💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial.
  • A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website. The real questions appear when someone rotates it, loads it on a typical connection, or views it on a narrow phone screen. AI generators have made the first draft of a model cheap, which shifts the work toward the part developers and designers already know: budgets, testing and fallbacks.

Recent findings suggest that this article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example. The checks apply equally to output from other generators. It includes a small Node.js script that audits a GLB file against a size budget, and the markup for a lightweight viewer with a static fallback. The model shown is one candidate, so it cannot prove browser speed, mobile behavior, hidden geometry or export compatibility. Those are checks to run on your own asset.

Sources indicate that traditional 3D work involves modeling, polygon layout, materials, scale and export. AI generation can shorten the blank-workspace stage. A beginner may discover the category through a search such as AI 3D model generator free, but an initial candidate is useful only if it survives review.

Recent findings suggest that for this vessel, start with the negative space, meaning the openings between the ribs. A flattering front view can hide a blocked cavity, a thin wall, or two surfaces passing through each other. Generation moves the bottleneck from making a first shape to deciding whether that shape is usable.

It has been revealed that image-to-3D tools use a visual reference to create a model candidate, while text-to-3D routes start from a written prompt. Tripo offers both, and other hosted options include Meshy, Rodin by Hyper3D and 3D AI Studio, all of which list GLB among their export formats, while open-source models such as TripoSR and Stable Fast 3D let you run generation yourself. Features, pricing, licensing and output quality differ and change often, so check each vendor’s current documentation. The image route suits this example because the folds, uneven rim and openings already exist in the source.

Whichever tool you use, it can provide a candidate for inspection. It cannot decide whether the source is licensed, whether the unseen rear structure is believable, or whether the exported asset suits a particular viewer. Those judgments belong to the person publishing the page.

According to recent reports, give the object one job. In a portfolio, this vessel might show how its shell and openings relate. That is narrower than calling it printable, manufacturable or dimensionally accurate. Note what must remain recognizable, and provide a still image if the interactive view fails.

Industry observers note that use an image you own or have permission to reuse. Busy backgrounds can distract an image-based workflow, so isolate the object when possible. One photograph also leaves the back and underside unknown. Treat those areas as review risks, not as details confirmed by the source.

After generation, rotate beyond the familiar front. Check the rear, top, underside and sides. Trace each large opening. Look for merged ribs, intersecting surfaces or an unstable base. A wireframe view, when available, can expose crowded geometry. A single front-facing candidate cannot answer these hidden-angle questions, so check them on your own model.

Record the download size, polygon count and texture dimensions. Polygons are the small flat faces that form the shape, and web viewers draw them as triangles. This matters because generator defaults are often tuned for quality, not for the web. In the generation screenshot for this vessel, the viewer reports roughly 1.95 million faces and the settings show 4K texture quality. That is a fine starting point for inspection but a heavy asset for a phone on a mobile connection. Curved ribs may need many triangles, but the count should still fit your page budget.

In a recent development, glTF is the open format most web viewers expect, and GLB is its single-file form that can bundle geometry, textures and materials. The format does not guarantee good performance, so measure the package. The script below reads a GLB with the open-source glTF Transform library, counts triangles, lists texture sizes, and compares them with a budget. The budget values are placeholders; set your own from your target devices.

Run it with node audit.mjs model.glb after installing @gltf-transform/core. It exits with a non-zero status when the asset is over budget, so you can run it in CI. A short test builds two GLBs with known triangle counts, one small and one with 200,000 triangles, and checks that the first passes and the second fails with the right message:.

When an asset fails, glTF Transform also has a command line. gltf-transform inspect model.glb reports what is inside a file, and gltf-transform optimize input.glb output.glb --compress draco --texture-compress webp applies geometry and texture compression. Compression and mesh simplification can introduce artifacts, especially around thin ribs and openings, so reopen the result and re-check the angles from Gate 3 instead of accepting a smaller file blindly. Also check that your viewer supports the compression you choose.

Industry observers note that load the asset in the intended viewer at desktop and phone widths. Check framing, touch rotation, keyboard access, scrolling and a slower connection. The Google-backed model-viewer web component is one low-code option, and libraries such as three.js give you more control at the cost of more code. The markup below shows the pieces that matter for a first release: a poster image that loads first, lazy loading so the heavy file waits until needed, a text alternative, and visible controls.

The alt text, a poster and touch-action="pan-y" (so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page on a phone) address the common failures. Check the current model-viewer documentation for attribute names and the recommended script include, since they can change between versions. Also consider the WCAG guidance on non-text content: provide a useful description, and offer instructions plus a static image for people who cannot operate the viewer.

In a recent development, A single front-facing candidate is enough to discuss the method, not to certify a finished web asset. Call it a prototype until the exported file passes the checks required by its actual destination.

The same review pattern can be adapted to an architectural ornament, exhibition object, packaging concept or game prop, but each destination adds its own geometry, scale and delivery requirements. A portfolio may accept an inferred rear surface if that limitation is clear. A sales page, printable file or measured product needs stronger references and technical validation.

The audit script counts triangles, texture sizes and file size only. It does not detect self-intersections, thin walls, flipped normals or licensing problems, and passing it does not make an asset good. The budget numbers are illustrative, and real limits depend on your audience’s devices and connections. Tool features and terms change, so verify them with the vendor before you rely on them, and treat any speed or quality claims on vendor pages as the vendor’s own.

Inspect the angle you would normally crop out. Confirm input rights, measure the download, and test touch, keyboard and a slow connection. Reread the surrounding copy, because claims of fabrication accuracy or production readiness need supporting evidence. For this vessel, “exploratory web model” is an honest label, and more demanding claims require better references and a specialist review.

Industry observers note that decide what visitors should learn or do before adding a 3D viewer. A modest prototype with a useful fallback can beat a dramatic asset that loads slowly or hides limitations.

Do I need to code to create a model with an AI generator? No code is required to generate an initial model candidate in Tripo or similar tools. Publishing it interactively is separate work and usually involves a viewer, hosting, responsive testing and enough HTML or JavaScript knowledge to diagnose problems.

According to recent reports, when should I use image-to-3D instead of text-to-3D? Use image-to-3D when a rights-cleared visual should guide the form, and text-to-3D when the idea begins as words. Do not treat the two routes as interchangeable evidence.

In a recent development, is a generated model ready to publish as soon as it exports? No. Inspect the shape from several angles, measure the delivery package, test the intended viewer and prepare a fallback. Higher-stakes uses may also need specialist geometry, scale, material and rights review.

How can a beginner keep web 3D manageable? Give one object one clear job. Set a file-size target, test desktop and phone widths, keep interaction simple, and retain a still image for readers who cannot load or operate the viewer.

Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because company president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action.

The USA’s latest ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.

Speaking on the manufacturer’s Q3 earnings call, Lau said the newly introduced US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.

Sources indicate that “It does set everyone back. It sets everyone back in China,” Lau said. “So everyone is actually having less advanced compute to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China.”.

He stated the ban will impact Tencent’s ability to train models.

Sources indicate that “Our training efficiency with Hy4 is actually very high,” he mentioned. “When we look at the next version, it would take probably longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.”.

“But over time, the domestic supply chain would actually come on board.”.

Lau also thinks the bans won’t hamper Tencent’s ability to run inferencing workloads, because made-in-China chips “should be able to cover it.”.

According to recent reports, “And over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we see the industry is progressing very fast,” he added. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to actually speed up even further, because all the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”.

Tencent needs GPUs, and lots of them, because the 10 million users of its agentic assistant WorkBuddy are collectively consuming over 100 trillion tokens per day. Lau thinks WorkBuddy is on track to becoming a hit product, partly because many users are outside China.

Lau stated Tencent can serve WorkBuddy customers outside China because the service can operate with different models, and the company thinks it can find third parties to provide the necessary inferencing services without the new US bans creating a problem.

But Lau remarked that GPU rentals and other cloud services, which are also growing strongly, may be impacted.

“In terms of cloud, if it is non-GPU related, we can actually build capacities ourselves outside of China,” he said. “I think there is still a lot of such opportunities because our cloud service is actually very cost competitive. When it comes to GPU, then unfortunately, we cannot actually offer high-end GPU anymore. We may be able to work with some partners in different places.”.

It has been revealed that tencent doesn’t break out revenue for its cloud services, but remarked they rose by 35 percent year-on-year, well ahead of the tech giant’s overall eight percent growth. Marketing services also grew strongly, by 19 percent, thanks in part to upcoming AI-powered systems that improve ad targeting.

The organization’s WeChat and Weixin messaging platforms continued to grow, adding 35 million accounts to exiting the quarter with 1.44 billion monthly active users.

One Tencent biz that went backwards was its international gaming unit, which saw revenue fall nine percent.

Chief strategy officer James Mitchell stated that slowdown wasn’t caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. “I think that in fairness, the slowdown for us predated the run-up to GTA VI,” he said, before predicting that Tencent’s existing and future “evergreen games” should help to turn things around.

According to recent reports, “The game environment globally is one where the rate of innovation has slowed somewhat, and now with AI, there’s opportunities to re-accelerate innovation,” he said. ®.

Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win.
  • Recent findings suggest that except it’s not.
  • We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

Recent findings suggest that except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem promptly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

In a recent development, across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

The explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

It has been revealed that the takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

First, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Industry observers note that second, even if you could perfectly estimate difficulty, it’s only one signal among many. In production, routers need to balance cost, latency, model specialization, and reliability simultaneously. Enterprise deployments pile on more: compliance requirements, data residency rules, privacy constraints, approved model lists. A task that would ideally go to one model might need to go elsewhere because of governance — and the router has to handle that gracefully.

Routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

According to recent reports, it’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

According to recent reports, routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Industry observers note that then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

According to recent reports, the figure below shows the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The key thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

Industry observers note that notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

According to recent reports, agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.

Sources indicate that it was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

For example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

It has been revealed that before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

On the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

But there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically, is not a presentational element like a . It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:.

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like and , they don’t bring in the connection that and have, and it’s better to reserve and for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

So, is it okay if I use this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:.

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):.

…changes to this (for the table markup):.

Recent findings suggest that to me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

If you've worked with named entity recognition (NER) in text, you've probably seen BIO tagging before. It's the standard way to mark where entities start, continue, and end inside a sequence of tokens. What you might not know is that the same tagging scheme has become the backbone of document AI -- the field where machine learning models extract structured data from invoices, receipts, contracts, and other business documents.

This guide explains how BIO tagging works, why it matters for document understanding, and how to build BIO-tagged training data that actually produces accurate models. We'll walk through the tagging logic, show real examples on financial documents, cover common mistakes that silently hurt model performance, and look at tools that speed up the annotation process.

BIO stands for Beginning, Inside, Outside. It's a labeling scheme that tells a model which tokens belong to an entity, which tokens continue that entity, and which tokens are just background noise.

● B (Beginning) -- the first token of a named entity.

● I (Inside) -- any token that continues the same entity.

● O (Outside) -- any token that doesn't belong to any entity.

Sources indicate that take a simple line from an invoice: "Invoice #INV-2024-0891". If you're labeling invoice numbers, the BIO tags look like this:.

Token          Label ─────          ───── Invoice        O #              O INV-2024-0891  B-invoice_number.

According to recent reports, now consider a multi-word entity like a vendor name: "Acme Corporation Ltd". All three words are part of the same entity, so the tagging becomes:.

Token          Label ─────          ───── Acme           B-vendor_name Corporation    I-vendor_name Ltd            I-vendor_name.

The B prefix marks where the entity starts. The I prefix marks every following token that belongs to the same entity. Everything else gets O. This three-label structure is simple, but it gives models enough information to learn entity boundaries precisely -- even when two entities of the same type appear next to each other.

Traditional NER works on plain text -- a flat sequence of words. Document AI is harder because pages have two dimensions. A word's meaning depends not just on what comes before and after it in reading order, but also on where it sits on the page. The number "$4,250.00" could be an invoice total, a line item price, or a tax amount depending on its position relative to headers and columns.

Industry observers note that models like LayoutLMv3, LiLT, and BROS solve this by combining text tokens with their bounding box coordinates. Each token gets three inputs: the word itself, its position on the page (x, y, width, height), and its BIO label during training. The model learns to associate spatial patterns with entity types.

According to recent reports, BIO tagging fits this architecture perfectly because it operates at the token level. Every word on the page gets exactly one label, and the model learns from thousands of these labeled tokens which spatial and textual patterns correspond to which fields.

If you're coming from a background in natural language processing in Python, the concept is identical -- BIO tagging works the same way whether your tokens come from a sentence or a document page. The difference is that document AI adds positional data to each token.

BIO isn't the only tagging scheme. You'll encounter several variants:.

● BIO (IOB2) -- B marks the first token, I marks continuation tokens, O marks non-entities. The most widely used scheme.

● BIOES -- adds E (End) for the last token of a multi-word entity and S (Single) for single-token entities. More explicit boundary marking.

● BILOU -- adds L (Last) and U (Unit). Functionally identical to BIOES with different letters.

Industry observers note that ● IOB1 -- the original scheme where B is only used when two entities of the same type are adjacent. Rarely used today.

According to recent reports, for document AI, standard BIO (IOB2) is the safest choice. Here's why:.

● LayoutLMv3 and most pre-trained document models expect BIO format out of the box.

● The FUNSD and CORD benchmark datasets use BIO, so your data format matches the academic baselines.

● BIOES adds more label types, which means you need more training data to learn each one reliably.

● Converting from BIO to BIOES is trivial if you later need it, but the reverse can lose information.

Unless your model architecture specifically requires BIOES or BILOU, stick with BIO.

Before you tag a single token, you need a clear label taxonomy -- the list of entity types your model will learn to recognize. A poorly designed taxonomy creates confusion during annotation and cascades into model errors.

Sources indicate that ask yourself: what fields does the downstream system need? For invoice processing, a typical taxonomy looks like this:.

vendor_name vendor_address invoice_number invoice_date due_date line_item_description line_item_quantity line_item_price subtotal tax total payment_method currency.

**Rule 1 -- One label per semantic meaning. **Don't reuse amount for both line item prices and the invoice total. A model that learns "amount" means two different things depending on context will confuse them on novel layouts.

**Rule 2 -- Use hierarchical names. **Once your taxonomy exceeds 10 labels, flat names start colliding. line_item_price is better than price because it's self-documenting and prevents collisions with total_price.

**Rule 3 -- Include a catch-all label. **Call it other or O. Text that doesn't belong to any entity still needs a label for token classification. Without negative examples, the model can't learn what isn't a field.

It has been revealed that **Rule 4 -- Match your model architecture. **Token classification models like LayoutLMv3 work best with fine-grained, word-level labels. Generative models like Donut output structured text, so they work with coarser labels. Choose your model first, then design labels to match.

Here's the practical workflow for turning raw PDF documents into BIO-tagged training data ready for model training.

According to recent reports, your model needs both the text and its coordinates on the page. For digitally generated PDFs, extract the text layer directly:.

import pdfplumber def extract_words(pdf_path):     words = []     with pdfplumber.open(pdf_path) as pdf:         for page in pdf.pages:             for word in page.extract_words():                 words.append({                     'text': word['text'],                     'bbox': [word['x0'], word['top'],                              word['x1'], word['bottom']],                     'page': page.page_number                 })     return words.

For scanned documents, you'll need OCR. Tesseract is the standard open-source option:.

import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path def ocr_pdf(pdf_path, dpi=300):     images = convert_from_path(pdf_path, dpi=dpi)     all_words = []     for i, img in enumerate(images):         data = pytesseract.image_to_data(             img, output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT         )         for j in range(len(data['text'])):             if data['text'][j].strip():                 all_words.append({                     'text': data['text'][j],                     'bbox': [data['left'][j], data['top'][j],                              data['left'][j] + data['width'][j],                              data['top'][j] + data['height'][j]],                     'page': i + 1                 })     return all_words.

Models expect coordinates normalized to a 0--1000 range. This makes the model resolution-independent -- a word at the top-left corner is at (0, 0) whether the page is 72 DPI or 300 DPI.

def normalize_bbox(bbox, page_width, page_height):     return [         int(1000 bbox[0] / page_width), *        int(1000 *bbox[1] / page_height),         int(1000 bbox[2] / page_width), *        int(1000 *bbox[3] / page_height)     ].

If you've worked with bounding box annotation for document AI, you'll recognize this normalization step -- it's the same coordinate transformation used across all document understanding models.

This is the annotation step. For each word in the document, assign the appropriate BIO label based on what field it represents. Here's what a fully labeled invoice line looks like:.

words = [     {'text': 'Invoice',      'label': 'O'},     {'text': 'Date:',        'label': 'O'},     {'text': 'March',        'label': 'B-invoice_date'},     {'text': '15,',          'label': 'I-invoice_date'},     {'text': '2024',         'label': 'I-invoice_date'},     {'text': 'Total:',       'label': 'O'},     {'text': '$4,250.00',    'label': 'B-total'},     {'text': 'Acme',         'label': 'B-vendor_name'},     {'text': 'Corporation',  'label': 'I-vendor_name'}, ].

Notice that "March 15, 2024" is a single entity spanning three tokens. The first token gets B-invoice_date, and the following tokens get I-invoice_date. The model learns that these tokens form one continuous entity.

LayoutLMv3 expects training data in a specific JSON structure. Each document becomes one training example with parallel arrays for words, bounding boxes, and labels:.

{   "id": "invoice_001",   "words": ["Invoice", "Date:", "March", "15,", "2024",              "Total:", "$4,250.00", "Acme", "Corporation"],   "bboxes": [[84, 42, 145, 58], [84, 62, 120, 78],              [130, 62, 172, 78], [175, 62, 195, 78],              [198, 62, 230, 78], [84, 320, 125, 336],              [130, 320, 210, 336], [84, 22, 125, 38],              [130, 22, 210, 38]],   "labels": ["O", "O", "B-invoice_date", "I-invoice_date",              "I-invoice_date", "O", "B-total",              "B-vendor_name", "I-vendor_name"] }.

If you're working with large volumes of documents, this guide on building JSON training datasets from PDFs covers how to automate much of this conversion pipeline.

Manually labeling every word on every page is slow. A single invoice might have 200-400 tokens, and you need hundreds of labeled documents for a usable model. Here are three approaches to speed things up.

Many financial fields follow predictable patterns. Dates, currency amounts, and invoice numbers can be pre-labeled with regex before a human annotator reviews them:.

import re PATTERNS = {     'invoice_date': [         r'\b\d{1,2}[/-]\d{1,2}[/-]\d{2,4}\b',         r'\b(?:Jan|Feb|Mar|Apr|May|Jun|Jul|Aug|Sep|Oct|Nov|Dec)\w*\s+\d{1,2},?\s+\d{4}\b'     ],     'total': [         r'$[\d,]+.\d{2}\b'     ],     'invoice_number': [         r'\b(?:INV|inv)[- ]?\d{4,}\b'     ] } def pre_label(words):     for word in words:         word['label'] = 'O'  # default         for label, patterns in PATTERNS.items():             for pattern in patterns:                 if re.match(pattern, word['text']):                     word['label'] = f'B-{label}'                     break     return words.

This won't catch everything -- vendor names, addresses, and line item descriptions need human judgment. But it can pre-fill 30-40% of the labels on a typical invoice, turning the annotator's job from labeling to reviewing.

In a recent development, train a preliminary model on your first 50 labeled documents, then use it to predict labels on upcoming documents. The annotator reviews and corrects the predictions instead of labeling from scratch. As the model improves, corrections become rarer and annotation speed increases.

The key is selecting documents where the model is least confident for the next round of human review. This focuses annotator time where it has the most impact on model accuracy.

If you're working with standard financial documents and want to skip the manual pipeline entirely, platforms like AI Asset Management can auto-generate structured labels from raw PDFs -- typically returning results in under 30 seconds per document. The annotator's role shifts from labeling to quality review, which is significantly faster than tagging every token by hand.

In a recent development, these are the errors that show up most often when teams start building document AI training data. Each one silently degrades model performance.

Sources indicate that if "Acme Corporation" is labeled as one entity on page 1 but "Acme" and "Corporation" are labeled as separate entities on page 5, the model receives contradictory training signals. Pick a convention and enforce it across your entire dataset. For vendor names, include the full legal name ("Acme Corporation Ltd") every time.

A common beginner mistake is labeling every token of a multi-word entity with B instead of using B for the first token and I for the rest. "March 15, 2024" should be B-date, I-date, I-date -- not B-date, B-date, B-date. The B-B-B pattern tells the model these are three separate entities, which is wrong.

Sources indicate that the word "Total:" is a header, not a value. Only the actual value ($4,250.00) should be tagged as B-total. Labeling "Total:" as part of the entity teaches the model to include headers in its extractions, which corrupts downstream processing.

Some OCR engines split punctuation into separate tokens. "$4,250.00" might become ["$", "4,250", ".", "00"]. If you label only "4,250" and skip the dollar sign and cents, the model learns incomplete extraction patterns. Make sure every token in the entity is covered by B or I tags.

Industry observers note that if 95% of your tokens are labeled O and only 0.5% are B-invoice_number, the model will learn that predicting O is almost always correct. This is the class imbalance problem. It's normal for O to dominate, but watch for entity types that appear in fewer than 1% of tokens -- those need more training examples or the model won't learn them reliably.

Recent findings suggest that before you start training, run these checks on your labeled data. Catching errors here is cheaper than debugging a confused model later.

An I-vendor_name tag should never appear without a preceding B-vendor_name. If it does, either the B tag was missed or the entity boundaries are wrong.

def validate_bio_sequences(labels):     errors = []     for i, label in enumerate(labels):         if label.startswith('I-'):             entity_type = label[2:]             if i == 0:                 errors.append(f'I-{entity_type} at position 0 with no preceding B tag')             else:                 prev = labels[i - 1]                 if prev != f'B-{entity_type}' and prev != f'I-{entity_type}':                     errors.append(f'I-{entity_type} at position {i} follows {prev}')     return errors.

Count how many times each label appears across your dataset. Flag any entity type that appears in fewer than 1% of total labels -- it likely needs more training examples.

from collections import Counter def check_distribution(all_labels):     counts = Counter(all_labels)     total = sum(counts.values())     for label, count in counts.most_common():         pct = 100 count / total *        flag = ' ** RARE **' if pct < 1.0 and label != 'O' else ''         print(f'  {label}: {count} ({pct:.1f}%){flag}').

Coordinates should fall within the page dimensions, and no bounding box should have zero or negative width or height:.

def validate_bboxes(words, page_w=1000, page_h=1000):     issues = []     for w in words:         x0, y0, x1, y1 = w['bbox']         if x1 <= x0 or y1 <= y0:             issues.append(f"Zero/negative size: {w['text']}")         if x0 < 0 or y0 < 0 or x1 > page_w or y1 > page_h:             issues.append(f"Out of bounds: {w['text']}")     return issues.

This depends on your document diversity and label count, but here are practical benchmarks based on fine-tuning LayoutLMv3 from a pre-trained checkpoint:.

Single layout (e.g., one vendor's invoices).

Good accuracy on similar layouts.

Multi-type (invoices + receipts).

These numbers assume fine-tuning from a pre-trained checkpoint, not training from scratch. Starting with a checkpoint like LayoutLMv3-base gives you document layout understanding for free -- your BIO-tagged data just teaches it which fields to extract from your specific document types.

Industry observers note that start small. Label 50 documents, train a model, check the error patterns, fix your taxonomy if needed, then scale up. Labeling 1,000 documents with a flawed taxonomy wastes more time than labeling 50 documents twice.

Once your data is tagged and validated, the training pipeline is straightforward. Here's the outline using Hugging Face Transformers:.

from transformers import (     LayoutLMv3ForTokenClassification,     LayoutLMv3Processor,     TrainingArguments,     Trainer ) \.

model = LayoutLMv3ForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(     'microsoft/layoutlmv3-base',     num_labels=len(label_list)  # your BIO labels ) \.

args = TrainingArguments(     output_dir='./results',     num_train_epochs=30,     per_device_train_batch_size=4,     learning_rate=5e-5,     evaluation_strategy='epoch',     save_strategy='epoch',     load_best_model_at_end=True ) \.

trainer = Trainer(     model=model,     args=args,     train_dataset=train_data,     eval_dataset=val_data ) trainer.train().

It has been revealed that the key hyperparameters to tune are learning rate (start with 5e-5), batch size (4 or 8 depending on GPU memory), and number of epochs (30 is a good starting point for small datasets). Use an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split, and make sure document types are distributed across all three splits.

● BIO tagging assigns B (beginning), I (inside), or O (outside) to every token. It's the standard labeling scheme for token classification in document AI.

● Pair BIO labels with normalized bounding box coordinates so models learn both textual and spatial patterns.

Sources indicate that ● Design your label taxonomy before you start annotating. One label per semantic meaning, hierarchical names, and a catch-all O label.

● Validate early. Check BIO sequence integrity, label distribution, and bounding box coordinates before training.

Sources indicate that ● Start with 50-100 labeled documents, train a model, check errors, and scale up. Quality matters more than quantity.

● Use pre-labeling (regex or model-based) to speed up annotation. Manual labeling from scratch doesn't scale.

The annotation step is the foundation of every document AI pipeline. The model you train is only as good as the BIO labels you feed it. Take the time to build a clean taxonomy, label consistently, and validate before training -- it saves debugging time later and produces models that actually work in production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At least it’s less disruptive than an internet shutdown.

At 08:30 on Thursday morning every powered-on mobile phone in South Korea blared out an Extreme Emergency Alert tone for 10.5 seconds – but the nation was at peace, with no major natural disasters occurring.

In a recent development, the extreme emergency South Korea hoped to avoid was cheating in the annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), an exam that over half a million people sit in the hope of securing admission to their preferred university. This year, around a third of those applicants are repeating the test after their previous effort didn’t get them the result they wanted.

It has been revealed that CSAT involves five separate examinations staged in a single day. Participants can only bring pencils to the test. Smartphones or any sort of tech is strictly forbidden.

Which is why Korean authorities used the national alert system on the day of CSAT, because if the 40dB tone sounded in an exam centre, it could indicate a student had deliberately or inadvertently tried to bring a smartphone – perhaps as an exam aide.

Korean media report the 08:30 alert turned up nine phones.

Authorities will send a second alert tone at an unspecified time later in the day to again smoke out any surreptitious smartphones.

It’s not possible to opt out of the alerts, one reason a concerned netizen has used the Android concern tracker to suggest sending alerts to detect exam cheats could be an abuse of the emergency alert system that Google might want to do something about.

South Korea sends a lot of emergency alerts, for matters such as helping to find missing persons or to warn of dangerous weather. It’s not uncommon to receive several in a single day. Authorities also gave advance notice of the CSAT alerts, which will not, therefore, cause panic on the streets of Seoul or Busan.

In a recent development, CSAT day is, however, a serious occasion. Some businesses open late so test-takers can get to their exams without having to battle peak hour traffic.

Those measures are arguably less disruptive than the widespread internet outages that some states in India impose on major exam days.

It has been revealed that an alleged leak of one Indian exam paper saw the nation’s tech regulator ban messaging service Telegram in the country and eventually sparked a youth protest movement that Newly introduced Delhi tried to suppress with more deliberate internet outages. ®.

Security incident disclosure — July 2026

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure.
  • We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services.
  • Recent findings suggest that the intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one key way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

Recent findings suggest that the intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

According to recent reports, the campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the concern and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

Recent findings suggest that we are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

Sources indicate that the attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

According to recent reports, when we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Recent findings suggest that autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

Industry observers note that cool. How did you guys learned to do this? there is no "this is how to use LLM to protect yourself, university". I wish i knew 1/100th of what average LLM customers know.

It has been revealed that the technique is documented in articles on ArXiv and other places. This is one of the first documented instances though.

Sources indicate that literally the plot of terminator 2. Glad to hear you guys were able to identify and fix the problem.The use of GLM 5.2 is promising.

It is great strategy in defence.

“ We ran the forensic analysis instead on GLM 5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.”.

Hyperscalers and (X)Lab-spying-API services stock just dropped another -20%.

Now we all get to wonder how exactly they are doing this with open weights/system prompt modifications.

Is there anyway or notification feed to receive future notification of security incidents please?

Thanks for sharing. Not enough people realize this is the future threat landscape. The big takeaway for me is that unless you're a Fortune 500, OpenAnthropic and ClaudeGPT probably aren't coming to save you when this happens. You guys are Huggingface, you have a few GPUs to spend when you get hacked. For the little guys and gals who might be targeted like this down the road: is Qwen 3.6 27B "enough" to analyze an attack like this usefully? Or are we flapping in the breeze if we don't have an 8xB300 server with 2+GB VRAM? Obviously a system with >2TB of VRAM is "nice to have" if you're hacked, but if you're comparatively GPU-poor is it worth building a response capability?

You can run GLM 5.2 on 4 sparks with more than enough context to perform DFIR analysis and it does not cost a fortune.

check your MCP connections too, they need second auth handshakes for correctness, otherwise your zero-GPUs will service outside.

It has been revealed that mojtaba Seyedi demonstrated how to build a scrollspy with modern CSS. What’s a scrollspy, you ask? Well, if you have a navigation that links to different sections of the page, a scrollspy highlights the section that you’re right now on in the navigation.

Brecht De Ruyte showcased and explained some absolutely stunning random() demos.

Okay, that was more than a few….

According to recent reports, lea Verou explained, in detail, the different ways of implementing icons on the web. Many exciting CSS features of the future are mentioned, including Linked Parameters, ident(), @mixin and @apply, the @property shorthand, and more, so it’s a really deep dive with a lot of intrigue.

Kilian Valkhof suggested a universal pseudo-selector. I mean, the universal selector (*) doesn’t select pseudo-elements, which is why almost every website uses the following CSS snippet, right?

But there are way more of them now (e.g., ::backdrop and ::details-content, to name just a couple of common ones in the context of box-sizing: border-box), so Kilian suggests ::*.

In a recent development, declan Chidlow told us which fresh HTML and CSS features are useful for design systems. My favorites are text-box, sibling-index(), sibling-count(), @scope, and @custom-media, which are very handy even outside of design systems.

#69822. GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'

GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multiple CDNs and routing users to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.
  • For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first newly introduced instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple CDNs and routing users to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone.

Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.

For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first newly introduced instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release. Anecdotal evidence suggests fans of the game may today report they suddenly feel unfit to perform paid work.

Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19th.

Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network.

RIPE data scientist Emile Aben, with help from staffers Alun Davies and James Cowie, went looking for GTA-related traffic and found some interesting patterns.

Industry observers note that aben observed that traffic to PlayStations mostly came from content delivery networks operated by AWS and Fastly. Microsoft relied on Fastly for over half of traffic flowing to Xboxes and used Akamai too, but eschewed AWS's CloudFront.

Sources indicate that the data scientist observed heavy use of “GeoDNS,” a technique that returns different IP addresses for a single domain request, depending on a user’s location. DNS’s designers didn’t intend that. Indeed, the RIPE trio point out that Paul Vixie, the computer scientist who earned his place in the Internet Hall of Fame for massive contributions to the DNS system, regarded things like GeoDNS as “stupid DNS tricks.”.

Whatever you think of GeoDNS, the RIPE researchers found that folks who were likely downloading GTA VI from Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul were each directed to different sites.

Their probe of a network in Shanghai, China, found “a very distinct long lookup-chain with a hostname that is associated with the Alibaba Cloud in the end that maps to six different IP addresses.”.

“This hints at specialised treatment for some countries/regions,” Aben wrote.

He also noted that Internet Exchange Points, the interconnect facilities that network operators use to exchange traffic and shorten paths, had to cope with record traffic during the download period – and seem to have handled the load.

Aben thinks the GTA VI download program offers a useful lesson.

“DNS helps steer each player towards a download server, while multiple CDNs share the work of delivering the files,” he wrote. “That distribution matters beyond gaming. On the open Internet, game downloads share routers and link capacity with all kinds of other traffic, including critical services.”.

“Keeping downloads local helps leave capacity on long-distance links free for other uses, making that enormous demand manageable.” ®.

Industry observers note that openAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Cursor are all sending webhooks now, and all four built them on Standard Webhooks, the open spec written by Svix. Downloads of the spec's npm package went from 1.7 million a month in September 2025 to 220 million a month presently.

In a recent development, this may be boring to hear for the nth time, but the reason is agents. An individual person checks on a running job a few times. An agent told to watch for changes checks every resource, every minute, for as long as it runs, and almost every one of those requests comes back with nothing fresh. An agent that starts a job, polls until it finishes, and then starts the next one spends most of its time waiting: six steps with 15 seconds of polling each add 90 seconds, even when every operation is fast. Polling more often adds load, and polling less often adds delay, so there's not really a sweet spot.

An event-driven API gets rid of that trade-off. It tells consumers when something changed or finished, so they stop asking. That matters most for work that runs for minutes or hours, like batch inference, fine-tuning, and video generation, and many APIs still don't offer it. Of the 57 AI APIs with long-running jobs that Svix reviewed for its State of Webhooks 2027 report, 19 make you poll for the result.

Industry observers note that webhooks are how most APIs push those events, and you can get a v1 out pretty fast. Making it dependable is an infrastructure problem, which is a class of problem that requires more time by default. Before you ship webhooks, you need an append-only event log behind every delivery, a fixed event format, signed payloads, retries with backoff, event IDs receivers can deduplicate on, per-endpoint isolation, and delivery logs your customers can read. If you skip one of these things, a customer is just going to bring it up later.

Each section below covers one of them with adaptable code, and Standard Webhooks works with existing verification libraries in most languages.

If the request handler that changes the data also sends the webhook, a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses the event, and nothing records that it should have gone out. A customer whose endpoint was down for longer than your retry window has no way to find out what they missed.

Industry observers note that both problems go away if you write each event to an append-only table, scoped per customer, in the same transaction as the change. Webhooks are delivered from that table, and the same table backs an HTTP endpoint customers can read from a cursor. Svix calls this design POKE (Publish Once, Kickoff Everywhere). Build the log first: a consumer who misses a webhook needs somewhere to resume from.

Every code path that changes state calls one helper inside its own transaction:.

Pass the helper the transaction handle. An insert through the connection pool commits separately, so you can end up with the event and no change, or the change and no event.

Industry observers note that the advisory lock prevents a subtler bug. Postgres assigns sequence values at insert time, but rows only become visible at commit. With two concurrent writers, a reader can see ID 102, store it as its cursor, and then never see ID 101 when the slower transaction commits. Holding a per-customer lock until commit makes each customer's events visible in ID order.

Reading the log is one indexed range query. The endpoint returns a cursor even when there are no fresh events, so a client can always store it and ask again later:.

Industry observers note that authenticate stands in for the middleware that already protects your API and sets req.customerId. That scoping stops one customer from reading another's events. A customer who was offline for a week asks for events after their last cursor and gets everything they missed, in order. Publish your retention period, since it limits how far back that works. The same log can also serve synthetic created events for existing records when a new integration needs to load its initial state.

Customers write handlers against your payloads, so you'll be supporting every field you ship.

Give each event an id, type, timestamp, and data. Use the log row's ID as the event ID so webhooks and the pull endpoint agree. Name types as a resource plus a past-tense action, like invoice.paid, and publish a catalog with an example payload for each type.

Emit an event for each state change a consumer would otherwise poll for. Deletions are the ones teams forget most. Long-running jobs need completion and failure events, such as export.completed and export.failed.

Adding a field is safe. Removing or renaming one breaks handlers, so ship a new type such as invoice.paid.v2 and keep sending the old one until customers have moved over.

According to recent reports, anyone who finds a customer's webhook URL can POST a fake invoice.paid to it. A signature lets the receiver confirm the request came from you, wasn't modified in transit, and isn't an old request being replayed.

Recent findings suggest that standard Webhooks signs the string id.timestamp.body with HMAC-SHA256, using a separate secret for each endpoint. Including the timestamp is what lets receivers reject old requests. Generate secrets with "whsec_" + crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64").

Send the result in three headers. The ID comes from the log and stays the same on every retry. The timestamp is the time of the current attempt, so each retry gets a fresh signature.

Receivers need the matching check, so put it in your docs:.

The function takes the raw body because frameworks that parse JSON and serialize it again change the bytes, and the signature stops matching. It compares with crypto.timingSafeEqual, since === returns faster on an early mismatch and leaks timing information. It rejects requests more than five minutes old to block replays. The signature header is a space-separated list so that during a secret rotation you can send one signature per secret and the receiver accepts either.

It has been revealed that that code highlights how the scheme works. In production, use a Standard Webhooks library on both ends. It implements the same algorithm:.

Receiving endpoints go down during deploys and outages, and they return errors when they're rate limited. If you only try once, each of those is a lost webhook.

Recent findings suggest that count any non-2xx response as a failure, redirects included. Following a redirect to an arbitrary host is a security problem in its own right. Count slow responses as failures too. The code below gives up after 15 seconds. Publish whatever limit you pick, because customer handlers have to respond within it.

These delays match the schedule Svix runs in production: eight attempts over a little more than 27 hours. The early retries cover restarts. The later ones give someone time to notice an outage and fix it. After each failure, pass the number of attempts so far to nextAttemptAt, and when it returns null, mark the delivery as failed. The event is still in the log, so once the customer fixes their server they can replay it or read it from the pull endpoint.

Store attempt state in a table next to the log. Timers in process memory disappear when the process restarts, and you don't need a message broker to avoid that.

It has been revealed that decide what happens to endpoints that never come back. Svix disables an endpoint after five days of continuous failure and emits an event so the sender can tell the customer. Pick your own threshold, notify the customer when you disable their endpoint, and let them turn it back on.

Retries mean some events arrive twice. Usually the receiver processed the event but timed out before you saw its response, so you sent it again. Senders accept this at-least-once behavior because the alternative is dropping events, and receivers handle the duplicates.

Receivers deduplicate on webhook-id, which doesn't change between retries. The insert that stores the event can also be the duplicate check:.

webhook_inbox needs a text primary key id and a jsonb column payload. The handler verifies the signature, stores the event, and returns 204. A background worker processes the inbox, so the handler responds well within the sender's timeout. express.raw gives the route the unparsed body that verification needs.

Industry observers note that put this pattern in your docs with a note about ordering. Events in the log have a fixed order, but webhook deliveries don't always arrive in it. A retried invoice.created can land after invoice.paid. Receivers should keep whichever event has the newer updated_at, or read the pull endpoint when they need strict ordering.

According to recent reports, with a shared worker pool, one customer's hanging endpoint can tie up every worker for the full timeout while other customers' events wait. Limit concurrent deliveries per endpoint, and slow down delivery to endpoints that keep failing.

According to recent reports, customer-supplied URLs are also an attack surface. Someone can register http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal hostname and get your servers to call your cloud metadata service or private network. This is server-side request forgery (SSRF). Resolve the hostname before connecting, reject private and loopback addresses, and don't follow redirects. The delivery code sets redirect: "manual" for this reason.

Without a self-serve view, every "did you send it?" question goes to an engineer who has to search logs.

Sources indicate that give customers a page to add and remove endpoints, choose event types, and rotate secrets. For each message, show every attempt with its timestamp, status code, and response body. The response body usually contains the customer's own error message. Add buttons to replay a failed message and to send a test event.

Expose the same operations in your API. Creating an endpoint and choosing its event types should take one authenticated request, because scripts and AI agents now set up a lot of integrations and can't click through a dashboard.

This is the biggest item here because it needs a UI, and it's the one teams most often leave out of the first release.

Industry observers note that you can build all of this yourself, and many teams have. It comes down to the fact that it's cheap to manage delivery for 99% of your webhooks, but it's nontrivial to guarantee it for 100% of them. This is also ignoring the UX side such as offering the customer portal for your customers to manage their webhooks in.

In a recent development, svix, which sponsored this article, handles webhook delivery. You keep the event log and decide what goes in it. A small relay reads new rows and passes each one to Svix:.

Svix also hosts the debugging portal. This call returns a single-use link where the customer can manage endpoints, read delivery logs, and replay messages:.
