#69819. Tech Report: Newer Models, Same Advantage

📅 16 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2097 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Newer Models, Same Advantage

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models.
  • In a recent development, the training pipeline was built in two stages.
  • According to recent reports, the combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

In a recent development, the training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

According to recent reports, the combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

Recent findings suggest that OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

According to recent reports, the proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

Industry observers note that this distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

It has been revealed that that concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Industry observers note that three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two upcoming OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

Sources indicate that processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'.

It has been revealed that these are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

According to recent reports, dharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

The examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

According to recent reports, when a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output.

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

The operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Recent findings suggest that mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

It has been revealed that supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

It has been revealed that DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

Industry observers note that the benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It has been revealed that it is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

Recent findings suggest that what changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

Sources indicate that this is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — fresh architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Sources indicate that better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Industry observers note that three months ago, we revealed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence.
  • Sources indicate that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an upgrade to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

Sources indicate that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Sources indicate that our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

Sources indicate that A reduction is a tree of floating-point additions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so changing the tree changes where rounding occurs. The effect is easier to expose in bfloat16, which retains less precision than float32.

Google periodically tables fresh AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon.".

"Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post.

Neon emerged after Google last week emitted Hydrogen, after delivering Carbon two weeks earlier and wafting Argon out the door in late September.

Unlike OpenAI's celestial more intuitive model naming scheme – Astra, Sol, Luna, and Terra – which maps celestial position to capability, Google's chemical soup doesn't suggest a specific hierarchy.

To judge by price, Carbon or Argon would be Google's top tier model, based on non-discounted price that takes effect next month, each priced at $4/M input tokens, $20/M output.

The Chocolate Factory refers to Carbon as "Our most capable reasoning model" while Argon is "Our efficient Gemini 4 frontier reasoning model … with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon across complex coding, agentic, math, and science tasks.".

In a recent development, yet Neon, the latest element in the mix, surpasses both in Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, scoring 61 compared to Carbon at 60, Hydrogen at 54, and Argon at 50. At the same time, Neon costs less, at $3/M input tokens and $15/M output.

That favorable pricing is all the more surprising in light of Google's willingness, as of two days ago, to let people of its Gemini services opt out of generative AI model training without losing their chat histories.

Kavukcuoglu evidently recognizes the need to clarify its model rankings, an issue addressed in a blog post section titled "Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family.".

In a recent development, "While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency," he explains. "Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.".

That may not really clarify which model is appropriate for which task and frankly Google is fine with that.

Sources indicate that as noted, Google Antigravity comes with an Orchestrator that decides how to spend your money for you by swapping models on the fly. As the tech giant describes it, a developer might start a task using Carbon, which would write a strategy, and hand the task off to Hydrogen to benefit from its token thrift.

In a recent development, antigravity does support model pinning, for those who know what they want. But Google, like other companies exploring model routing and orchestration, is fine with developers delegating decisions that affect billing to their trustworthy service provider. ®.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.
  • It has been revealed that robot learning has a supply problem.
  • Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

It has been revealed that robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

Recent findings suggest that but you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

In a recent development, UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

According to recent reports, grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

Recent findings suggest that we have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

Industry observers note that and while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

The family shares the same hardware DNA:.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right).

It has been revealed that components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Industry observers note that robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Sources indicate that press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :.

Dataset available on this HF Dataset.

Policy available on this HF Model.

It has been revealed that the data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

In a recent development, this release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset.

#69814. Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1414 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.
  • Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms.
  • As described in their paper, "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.

Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms.

As described in their paper, "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope.

What's more, these unrestrained models have been deployed through applications, GitHub projects, and model routing platforms like Open Router, and users of those apps or services may not be aware of the nature of the underlying LLM.

"Uncensored LLMs generally refer to LLMs whose content filtering or refusal safeguards are absent, removed, or weakened, allowing them to respond to requests that aligned models may refuse," the paper explains.

Zilong Lin, lead author and assistant professor of computer science at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, told The Register that open source LLM hosting platforms like Hugging Face play a similar role to code hosting services like GitHub, GitLab, and Codeberg in the open source community by enabling sharing, modification, and redistribution of code artifacts.

"However, unlike traditional software, whose behavior can often be examined through source code analysis, the safety alignment of LLMs is difficult to assess directly from their model files," Lin explained. "Evaluating whether an LLM has adequate safety safeguards typically requires deploying the model and testing its responses to potentially harmful prompts, which involves substantial computational and financial costs.".

Lin said this makes the identification and assessment of LLM safety particularly challenging, particularly given the large number of models available. That's why he and his colleagues chose to study the space through publicly available model metadata.

Even popular commercial LLMs that are purportedly "aligned" – to some standard not everyone accepts – may respond to prompts with content deemed harmful. The US Government Accountability Office just released a report that found Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini can be coaxed to provide information that would help with the planning of a terror attack.

To highlight the consequences of AI advice, the GAO points to news reports indicating that generative AI helped enable the creation of an explosive device in a January 2025 attack on a Las Vegas hotel and the planning of a February 2026 mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada.

The issue with open weight LLMs is that anyone with modest technical skills (or just cluelessly assisted by a compliant LLM) can apply techniques like toxic training/fine-tuning (TTFT) or de-aligned training/fine-tuning (DTFT) to datasets that haven't been safe, in order to produce models with reduced or removed refusal behavior. Examples include toxicqa-Llama2-13B and WizardLM-7B-Uncensored. A more recent technique called refusal-direction ablation (or abliteration, e.g., Daredevil-8B-abliterated) dilutes refusal training to make the model less likely to refuse requests.

In a recent development, uncensored (or simply less restrictive) models have legitimate uses, sometimes ironically because commercial models are insufficiently permissive and refuse legitimate security analysis. Hugging Face, for example, had to resort to using Z.ai's less rule-encumbered GLM-5.2 to analyze the hacking of its infrastructure by OpenAI's irresponsibly unsupervised AI agents.

But ULLMs can just as easily be misused to provide guidance about illegal activity, assist with malware development, or emit content that's harmful, malicious, or manipulative in some way.

"We identified more than 11,000 ULLMs appearing across multiple platforms, with Hugging Face serving as the dominant upstream source," Lin said in a blog post.

In a recent development, "This movement exposes an important governance gap: models can travel more easily than the information needed to assess their risks. Only about 13 percent of the ULLMs we identified carried moderation warnings, and security threat indicators were not consistently preserved across platforms.

"This creates a supply chain problem: a model can be copied across platforms while the information needed to understand its risks is lost along the way.".

The ULLMs were evaluated for text output and not images. The issues raised by text-to-image LLMs, such as the ability to generate illegal images (e.g. CSAM), were beyond the scope of this particular study.

According to recent reports, "The uncensored LLMs we evaluated were generally more likely to comply with harmful requests and generate harmful content than non-uncensored models," Lin stated. "Our evaluation covered 11 categories of harmful requests, including child abuse, illegal activities, and fraud.

"However, the ability of an individual model to generate harmful content varies depending on several factors, including its training data, development methods, and the extent to which its refusal direction has been ablated.".

Recent findings suggest that A small portion of these ULLMs (27 of them, which have been downloaded 136,000 times) exhibited threat indicators from security scans. Many of these, authors say, had signatures associated with malware, exhibited suspicious binary patterns, or contained unsafe deserialization mechanisms that could allow arbitrary code execution.

Industry observers note that the number of ULLMs has been rising rapidly, according to the paper, from about 100 per month in May 2023 to more than 1,000 per month presently. And some of these models have been downloaded millions of times. The uncensored model dolphin-2.9.1-yi-1.5-34b has more than 53 million downloads, and more than 4.8 million just last month.

The authors note that many ULLMs violate the licensing terms of the models on which they've been based, not that source code licensing has had any meaningful impact on the behavior of the AI industry.

Asked whether the safety concerns arising from the availability of ULLMs might prompt a replay of the 1990s when authorities tried to limit the availability of cryptographic code, Lin remarked, "It is difficult to predict whether model abliteration tools will face similar legal challenges.

"As shown in Section 5.1 of our paper, refusal-direction ablation (i.e., abliteration) appeared in 2024 and rapidly gained popularity within the open-source LLM community. Within approximately two years, a growing ecosystem of publicly available tools had emerged to support this technique.

"In the meantime, techniques for both removing and mitigating LLM safety alignment have also become active research topics in academia, with many researchers releasing open-source tools and artifacts to support their studies.".

Recent findings suggest that dealing with the risks posed by uncensored models isn't easy because it depends on divining the intent of the user's prompt. When is a question about terrorism intended as a initiative and when is it guidance for writing a thriller? When is a question about hacking intended for theft and when is it cybersecurity education?

Recent findings suggest that the current approach taken by commercial labs — limiting powerful models to favored paying insiders and offering hobbled models to the rest — doesn't work for those left out. Applying some similarly censorious regime to open weight models isn't likely to achieve any more success than efforts by law enforcement to make cryptography available only to "the good guys.".

Lin expects that greater transparency, auditability, and verification of models will help.

Industry observers note that "As discussed in Section 8 of our paper, our approach to identifying uncensored LLMs relies on publicly available model metadata, such as model cards, to identify models that explicitly disclose their uncensored characteristics," he mentioned. "Our findings demonstrate the value of such transparency for identifying potentially unsafe models.

"Regulatory frameworks have also increasingly emphasized AI documentation and transparency. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models to maintain technical documentation covering model characteristics, capabilities, limitations, and evaluation results. Similarly, the Colorado AI Act recognizes model cards and dataset cards as possible documentation supporting AI impact assessments.".

Hugging Face, in the process of being acquired by Nvidia, did not respond to a request for comment. Nor did Kaggle or John Snow Labs, the two other US-based companies named in the study.

According to Lin, the research findings were responsibly disclosed to Hugging Face, John Snow Labs, OpenCSG, Kaggle, ModelScope, and Open Router.

Asked whether any of the companies responded, Lin remarked, "We received a response from OpenCSG, which expressed appreciation for our work on identifying and measuring uncensored LLMs, stating that 'your research is meaningful and supports the development of a safe and trustworthy LLM ecosystem.'".

Sources indicate that openCSG, the report says, has committed to enhance its service based on the research findings. ®.

#69813. Breaking: Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1429 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1429 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • Sources indicate that use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Sources indicate that use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

Recent findings suggest that text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Industry observers note that viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

According to recent reports, container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

Sources indicate that line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Recent findings suggest that default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each fresh word from reshuffling the paragraph.

In a recent development, hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

In a recent development, punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

It has been revealed that the first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

In a recent development, light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

According to recent reports, mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

In a recent development, numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

The tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

Industry observers note that font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

It has been revealed that quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

The quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Sources indicate that default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

Industry observers note that font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

:where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

According to recent reports, :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

In a recent development, here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

Some of these rules are still too newly introduced for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

Bringing Nunchaku 4-bit Diffusion Inference to Diffusers

📅 23 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs.
  • Most of these backends are weight-only.
  • According to recent reports, SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

Most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

According to recent reports, SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

With current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize new architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

It has been revealed that first, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:.

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:.

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

It has been revealed that SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

The original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a upcoming model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Sources indicate that nunchaku Lite is the fresh integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:.

The trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

Industry observers note that if you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:.

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:.

Volta and Hopper GPUs are currently not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:.

Quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

Offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

According to recent reports, as shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel debuts, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

Always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:.

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:.

Sources indicate that once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other customers can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

In a recent development, note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

Sources indicate that FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:.

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:.

Recent findings suggest that this grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:.

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:.

It has been revealed that this is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

Structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A New Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:.

Nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize new architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

Industry observers note that if you quantize and publish a upcoming model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

To learn more, check out the following resources:.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to the Diffusers maintainers for reviews and guidance throughout the integration, and to the MIT HAN Lab / Nunchaku team for the original SVDQuant work. Thanks to Marc Sun for providing feedback on the blog post. Thanks to Álvaro Somoza for trying out nunchaku-lite and for providing feedback.

rootonchair is also grateful to SilverAI for supporting this work and providing the environment in which much of this development took place.

Industry News: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the organization’s kingdom

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don't leave your credentials out in public, where any visitor can see them.
  • In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene.
  • Recent findings suggest that our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security firm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't leave your credentials out in public, where any visitor can see them.

In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

Recent findings suggest that our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security firm. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

According to recent reports, during a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

"Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door.".

Recent findings suggest that espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

It has been revealed that once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

Recent findings suggest that the accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records.

Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa stated.

Recent findings suggest that after getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They promptly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information.

Sources indicate that "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®.
