💡 Key Takeaways
  • Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization issue got Digital Ocean ducking.
  • If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.
  • VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware notes means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this glitch to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization issue got Digital Ocean ducking.

If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware notes means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this glitch to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite.

VMware also wants its owners to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root.

The prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software.

The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

VMware plans to ship newly introduced versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol.

Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Terra Security says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov indicates he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to enhancement its Linux implementations. The manufacturer has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

According to recent reports, terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The organization believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an upgrade, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • According to recent reports, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting complications by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

According to recent reports, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting glitch by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Industry observers note that continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

In a recent development, for each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

It has been revealed that AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review complications, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

Recent findings suggest that I open one of my environments. The Complications tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

Recent findings suggest that the Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

According to recent reports, the Remediation section highlights a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the matter is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that challenges are built from.

The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated challenges in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#69762. Industry News: Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2678 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like.
  • Industry observers note that we built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios.
  • According to recent reports, one note on measurement before the numbers start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. This is ours.

Industry observers note that we built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios. On identical hardware, running identical workloads, GPU utilization rose by as much as 33 percentage points, and priority-weighted output rose in every one of them, by as much as 105%. Nothing about the hardware changed. What changed was the order in which allocation decisions get made.

According to recent reports, one note on measurement before the numbers start. Every gain below is expressed as improvement over the FIFO result on the same scenario. Utilization is reported in percentage points; value is reported as a percentage increase in priority-weighted output.

Sources indicate that "Keep the GPUs busy" is not a decision a system can execute. The decision is narrower and much harder: which GPU runs which job, in which timestep, at what priority. Formally it is one binary choice per combination of GPU, job and timestep, and the output is a grid — every GPU, across the whole scheduling horizon, with a job name in each cell or nothing at all.

Four workload types compete for that grid: training, real-time inference, batch inference, and quantization. They split into two allocation shapes, and the split is where the difficulty lives. Training, batch inference and quantization are batch-like: once started, each needs a contiguous block of GPUs held without interruption until the job finishes. Real-time inference is the opposite: elastic, driven by a demand curve that changes every timestep, growing and shrinking as traffic does.

According to recent reports, two incompatible shapes competing for the same hardware in the same timestep is the core problem. A second heterogeneity sits inside a single type: for the same base model, training jobs range from a few hours to several days, and from one GPU to dozens.

The comparison point throughout is a FIFO-based scheduler: real-time inference served from a fixed reservation, and every other job placed in arrival order, without regard for priority.

Recent findings suggest that under the right conditions, that is a reasonable policy. When the cluster has slack, allocation order costs nothing in utilization, everything fits regardless of sequence, so FIFO and anything more sophisticated fill the same fraction of the pool. Contention is where that ordering cost stops being invisible and starts costing capacity too. It then becomes expensive in two separate ways, and they are worth taking one at a time.

It has been revealed that the reservation. Real-time inference cannot wait for capacity; the GPUs have to be there the moment traffic needs them. A scheduler that places jobs in arrival order has no mechanism for releasing GPUs during a trough and reclaiming them before the next peak, so the only way to guarantee availability is to take each real-time application's maximum demand for the day and reserve that many GPUs for the whole day. The cost lands in every hour that is not the peak. An application needing six GPUs at midday and two at 4am holds all six for twenty-four hours, and the four idle GPUs are unavailable to any batch job for the entire day. They are not being used, and they are not free either. It is why the baseline sits near half the cluster in the two scenarios where reservation dominates: 51.6% in the mixed control and 53.6% in the training-heavy case. Roughly half a pool, with much of the idle half reserved rather than free. This cost is paid whether the cluster is contended or not — contention only makes it visible.

The ordering. Under real contention, which jobs fit at all depends on the order you place them, not just on how much capacity exists. Order is not a tiebreaker applied after the capacity question is settled. Order is a capacity decision. FIFO places each job as it arrives, without weighing what that job is worth and without checking what else still has to fit inside the horizon, so high-priority work waits behind whatever asked first and capacity gets committed in placements that later jobs cannot use.

According to recent reports, the two compound. The block held for the day's maximum real-time demand is off the table for every batch job in the queue, in every hour, and whatever remains is handed out in the order the requests happened to arrive.

It is the GPU equivalent of an airline assigning aircraft to whichever charter called first, then finding nothing left to fly the route that actually pays. And GPUs reserved all day for a peak lasting a couple of hours are the grounded aircraft from the previous piece in the most literal sense: on standby, earning nothing, unavailable to anyone else.

[Figure: side-by-side allocation grids — allocator above, FIFO below, same scenario].

Sources indicate that across five benchmark scenarios built for genuine contention, the allocator improved both axes at once. Utilization moved from a 52–85% band to a 72–88% band. Priority-weighted value rose between 24.6% and 105.1%, averaging 52%. Every scenario, both metrics, no tradeoff to explain away.

The strongest single case was a training-heavy workload on 8 GPUs: utilization went from 53.6% to 87.0%, and value more than doubled, up 105%. Thirty-three points of a fixed, already-depreciating asset, recovered by reclaiming reserved standby capacity and placing the rest in priority order. (This figure reflect a single baseline ordering.).

The allocator removes both behaviors. Real-time demand is treated as a curve rather than a ceiling, allocated against demand at each timestep, with batch-like work occupying the troughs, bounded by the cap on how many GPUs a real-time job may swap between consecutive timesteps. And batch-like jobs are placed by priority across the whole horizon instead of in the order they arrived. The rest of this piece is how.

Recent findings suggest that utilization measures occupancy: what fraction of available GPU-time is allocated to something. It carries no information about what that something is worth. One scenario pulls the two apart completely, and the gap runs in a direction that is easy to miss.

In the scale test, 30 jobs across 64 GPUs, FIFO and the allocator produced identical utilization, 44.9% each, and identical throughput, 27 of 30 jobs completed. The allocator delivered 15.9% more priority-weighted value. Every dashboard reads the same. The cluster produced materially different output.

An objective that does not price priority can fill the cluster to exactly the same level, finish exactly as many jobs, and still deliver less. The previous piece argued that occupancy is a poor read on whether a cluster is earning; this is the measured version of that claim.

Industry observers note that the alternative is not a longer list of heuristic rules. Some constraints only mean anything globally, and no local rule can express them: contiguous blocks, a budget for how much GPU churn is acceptable across the entire horizon, a guarantee that running work is never preempted. To honor those, the problem has to be written down as one thing.

Five constraints define a legal allocation:.

The objective function has two terms. Allocating a GPU to a batch-like job earns a reward equal to its priority multiplied by a time-decay weight. Failing to meet real-time demand incurs a penalty proportional to the size of the shortfall.

According to recent reports, the relative size of those weights is the entire service-level policy, expressed as one number. The real-time penalty weight is 5 to 10 times greater than the allocation weight. One unit of unmet real-time demand therefore costs what 5 to 10 GPU-timesteps of equal-priority batch work costs. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it means latency obligations are enforced inside the same optimization that places batch work, rather than by a separate autoscaler competing with the scheduler for the same GPUs.

Sources indicate that it is also what makes the elastic treatment of real-time demand safe. The allocator can hand a GPU to batch work during a trough because underserving real-time demand later is priced so far above whatever that batch work earns — the penalty, not a static reservation, is what protects availability.

The time weight decays across the horizon for a reason that only makes sense in an online system: by the next scheduling run, new jobs will have arrived. Capacity used now is worth more than capacity promised later.

The formal model defines what a legal, well-scored allocation looks like. Answering an incoming request is a separate job, and it belongs to a separate component. This is NP-hard combinatorial allocation, and the scheduler is re-invoked every time a job arrives, so the decision has to come back in the gap between two API requests. That latency budget is the fixed constraint the architecture is designed around, which is why a heuristic sits on the hot path and the formal model sits behind it as the specification the heuristic is built to satisfy.

According to recent reports, that heuristic is not a generic greedy allocator. Its rules are the formal model's structural constraints, which means every grid it produces is a legal allocation by construction. Not usually valid. Valid by design.

It has been revealed that that design, applied across the whole horizon rather than one arrival at a time, is what produces the utilization gain. The allocator sees every queued job before it places any of them, it can hold the free pool in shapes the remaining work can actually occupy, a batch job needing a contiguous block of a given size still has room when its turn comes. Priority decides who gets first claim on that room. FIFO has neither view: it commits capacity to whichever job asked first, and a job that arrives later and needs a specific shape may find nothing left that fits, so it goes unscheduled and the GPU-hours it would have consumed go unclaimed.

It runs in 1 to 2 milliseconds on the five contended scenarios, and 15 milliseconds at 64 GPUs and 30 jobs — fast enough to run on every incoming request.

Industry observers note that the system exposes two modes. Fast mode runs the allocator alone and returns its grid; this is the hot path. Full mode uses that grid as a starting point for the formal model, which attempts to improve on it — suited to periodic review rather than per-request decisions.

Utilization improved in every scenario but one, where it tied exactly. Value improved in all seven.

The scale test matters because it holds at size: 64 GPUs, 30 jobs, 15 milliseconds, 15.9% more value.

In a recent development, the uniform-priority test matters because it addresses the obvious skeptical reading. Override every job to identical priority, so that no priority signal distinguishes any of them, and the allocator still moves utilization from 76.8% to 87.5% and value up 23.1%. The gain is not purely an artifact of ordering by priority. Planning placements across the horizon contributes on its own.

Industry observers note that everything above assumes the scheduler knows how many GPU-hours each job needs and how much real-time traffic is coming. Both are predictions, not inputs, and a scheduler is only as good as they are.

Industry observers note that A single generic estimator does not work, because the four workload types have qualitatively different cost drivers. This is where the specialization argument from the previous piece reconnects: the same logic that makes a task-specific model outperform a generalist applies to the estimators feeding the scheduler.

Training is not one workload. It varies along two independent, freely combinable axes. Strategy determines how much of the model is updated (full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient methods like LoRA). Technique determines the optimization objective and the training loop (SFT, DPO, RLHF, RLVR, CPT). The differences are not marginal: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by up to 10,000× and GPU memory roughly 3× against full fine-tuning, on the same base model. DPO removes both the reward model and the sampling loop of RLHF. Estimating from model size alone averages across runs that differ by orders of magnitude, in exactly the two quantities the scheduler decides on, duration and GPU count. Our training forecaster conditions on 22 features, including a categorical variable distinguishing 10 concrete training variants.

It has been revealed that quantization is a schedulable job, not a background chore. Quantizing a single large model can consume hours of GPU time on hardware that other work is waiting for. It gets its own forecast, built from calibration tiers by parameter count, with distinct handling per algorithm (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) and a safety margin before rounding up to whole GPU-hours. Prior work in this area places quantization outside scheduling scope entirely.

Real-time inference is not estimated per job at all. It is forecast as a continuously recalibrated weekly demand profile, rebuilt from hourly traffic history and mapped to GPU counts under the same swap cost the formal model enforces. Forecast and optimizer therefore agree on what churn costs, rather than disagreeing and fighting each other. This forecast is what replaces peak reservation. A per-timestep demand curve is the only thing that lets the scheduler release GPUs during a trough with any confidence that they can be reclaimed before the next peak.

This closes back to the ordering argument. Better demand estimates are what make priority-aware placement possible in the first place, you cannot sequence jobs well without knowing what they will consume.

The obvious objection to all of this is that forecasts are wrong. What happens then?

The failure mode to avoid has a name worth borrowing: the end-of-world effect. An optimizer that cannot see past the end of its horizon makes present decisions that wreck the timesteps immediately outside it, because as far as the model is concerned, nothing exists after the horizon ends.

The architecture answers both problems at once. The scheduler optimizes a 24-hour horizon, but commits only the current timestep, and re-runs every 30 to 60 minutes. Run at 9am, and the 9am allocation is real; the initiative for 10am through 5pm exists only so that the 9am decision is made by a model that knows a future exists. The real 10am allocation comes from the 10am run, against fresh data.

Recent findings suggest that the consequence is that forecast error is absorbed by re-optimization instead of compounding. Each run inherits what is actually running and pins it in place, so successive looks revision rather than thrash.

Recent findings suggest that there is a secondary payoff. The horizon plan is itself a forecasting product: it surfaces real-time coverage risk and predictable idle windows before they arrive, which is useful whether or not those specific allocations are ever committed.

Sources indicate that this is also why the time-decay weight exists. By the next run, the workload mix will have changed.

Airlines did not solve utilization by computing an optimal schedule. They solved it by encoding operational discipline into the order things happen (turnaround sequence, maintenance windows, crew rostering) and letting that discipline compound.

It has been revealed that the same thing happened here. Thirty-three points of utilization in the hardest-packed scenario, and 52% more priority-weighted output on average, on the same hardware, with the same workloads, in a couple of milliseconds, came from encoding what the cluster physically permits into the order decisions get made. Structure beat sophistication.

It has been revealed that the previous piece argued that specialization and orchestration are two halves of one problem: specialization shrinks what each workload needs, and orchestration decides where the difference goes. Neither lever pays off alone. This is what the second half looks like when it is built.

The GPUs were already installed, already committed, already depreciating. The gain was in how we chose to spend them.

Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.
  • Industry observers note that every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched.
  • Industry observers note that this story is the opposite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Industry observers note that every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

Industry observers note that this story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

He named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

Recent findings suggest that what made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is firm source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

It has been revealed that the version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

In a recent development, his product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known complications go away. So he bumped the version.

This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

In a recent development, buaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

Industry observers note that the report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the upcoming PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party firm, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

Industry observers note that it is notable to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

The trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

Industry observers note that this engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

Recent findings suggest that what makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

Recent findings suggest that here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

It has been revealed that remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a latest teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

Recent findings suggest that buaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script.

According to recent reports, the script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log.

The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

Sources indicate that we split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

It has been revealed that inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:.

Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner.

Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:.

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE.

Industry observers note that ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline.

The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with.

Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.).

The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

It has been revealed that kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

BuaJi runs as before, just in a upcoming place with only two variables:.

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:.

Industry observers note that because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

In a recent development, it won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:.

It has been revealed that the log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this:.

In a recent development, the runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails.

Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

According to recent reports, what hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security matter, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

It has been revealed that never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

According to recent reports, clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

Recent findings suggest that every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

Recent findings suggest that as we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

Industry News: AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1428 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo.
  • Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.
  • The rest of the week had a sharper edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

It has been revealed that introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s introduces Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 newly introduced voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

It has been revealed that AWS introduces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Industry observers note that amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

It has been revealed that discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

It has been revealed that tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

Industry observers note that AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

It has been revealed that that’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

#69759. Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1186 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on.
  • Recent findings suggest that you might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results.
  • Sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

Recent findings suggest that you might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

Sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:.

Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

In a recent development, this fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

Industry observers note that git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

There is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

Recent findings suggest that A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

This workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

One sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

It has been revealed that those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

That independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

For a web app preview, ask the agent:.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:.

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

An API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

Recent findings suggest that A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

It has been revealed that the same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

According to recent reports, the checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

Sources indicate that when using the out-of-the-box Gemini Enterprise web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for Federated Connectors or custom agents appear automatically in the chat UI.

Industry observers note that in practice, however, many enterprises build their own Customer UI to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this, Customer BE calls the Gemini Enterprise StreamAssist API.

The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of Customer UI and Customer BE:.

This guide walks through the architecture, component flows, and runnable code for all three layers (Figure 1):.

Breaking: US let Nvidia and AMD sell bucketloads of chips to military-linked Chinese companies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.
  • The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.
  • That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.

The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.

BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.

But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies, the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.

Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.

Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The Latest York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.

One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”.

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.

Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.

Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.

Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday mentioned that fresh ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

According to recent reports, alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the tech giant’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu mentioned the newly introduced policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”.

“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure proposal,” he mentioned.

But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.

Alibaba’s Wu predicted his firm “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.

Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.

And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.

Sources indicate that that’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®.
