Rebuilding my local voice assistant pipeline

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Platypush

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I wrote an article a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in Platypush.
  • And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants - in 2024 (with Picovoice), in 2020 (diving into the legacy assistant.google integration, the now defunct assistant.alexa integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the original article in 2019 describing the Google Assistant integration.
  • For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I wrote an article a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in Platypush.

And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants - in 2024 (with Picovoice), in 2020 (diving into the legacy assistant.google integration, the now defunct assistant.alexa integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the original article in 2019 describing the Google Assistant integration.

For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.

After a bit of experimentation, I decided to swap and fine tune a few parts, and after a couple of days of trying the results are satisfying enough for me to write a short article about it.

Hotword detection- assistant.microwakeword (local).

Speech-to-text- assistant.openai (cloud)- assistant.vosk (local).

Generate response- openai (cloud or local).

Text-to-speech- tts.openai (cloud)- tts.piper (local).

Hotword detection- assistant.microwakeword (local).

Speech-to-text- assistant.openai (cloud)- assistant.vosk (local).

Generate response- openai (cloud or local).

Text-to-speech- tts.openai (cloud)- tts.piper (local).

Until recently I used assistant.openwakeword, which wraps openWakeWord.

It works, but the project has been quiet for a while and all of its pre-trained models are v0.1 files from 2023, mostly trained on synthetic speech.

In practice I was getting both false positives (the hotword triggering on background noise) and false negatives (the hotword not detected unless I was close to the microphone).

I added a new plugin, assistant.microwakeword, on top of microWakeWord through the pymicro-wakeword Python bindings.

microWakeWord is the engine used by ESPHome and Home Assistant Voice, its models are actively maintained, and the built-in models (okay_nabu, hey_jarvis, hey_mycroft, alexa) ship with the package — no download required.

The current official models are provided under the ESPHome micro-wake-word-models repository.

Custom models are supported too: drop a microWakeWord JSON manifest (with its .tflite model) in the plugin's models directory and reference it by name.

The plugin exposes the same API as assistant.openwakeword (same models, detection_threshold, frame_duration, patience_frames, input_device, input_volume parameters, same list_models action, same HotwordDetectedEvent), so switching is a matter of just changing the configuration to point to the latest plugin:.

assistant.openai records audio when a conversation starts and transcribes it through Whisper.

In a recent development, the tricky part has always been end-of-speech detection: knowing when the user has finished talking. The previous implementation used a per-frame boolean from WebRTC VAD, and any single frame classified as speech would reset the silence timer. With even a bit of background noise, phrases would only end when the maximum conversation duration was hit.

The audio preprocessing layer (AudioPreprocessor, shared by the STT integrations) has been reworked:.

According to recent reports, hysteresis + sliding window: a frame becomes speech above the VAD threshold and stays speech until its score drops by a margin, and the per-frame decisions are smoothed by majority vote over a 0.5s window. A single noise burst can no longer keep a conversation alive.

Adaptive noise floor: the background noise level is tracked over time, and frames that aren't louder than noise_floor_factor (default 2.0, ~6 dB) times the floor are never considered as speech.

On a synthetic benchmark (Piper-generated phrases mixed with babble and burst noise), the old settings kept conversations open for 6–10 seconds after the speech had ended; the new pipeline ends them 1.0–1.6 seconds after the last word, which is the configured conversation_end_timeout plus the smoothing lag.

It has been revealed that since the changes on Platypush have been performed directly in the AudioPreprocessor also used by other native speech-to-text engines, other speech-to-text plugins also benefit from them - e.g. if you use assistant.vosk for full on-device detection.

The transcribed phrase is processed by the openai plugin, which handles both the API key and the conversation context. By default the assistant renders the response through the configured tts_plugin; if the response ends with a question mark, the conversation continues with a follow-up.

Custom hooks can intercept phrases before the default response kicks in — for example, to handle home automation commands locally without an LLM round-trip:.

And the hotword event is wired to the conversation start with a similar hook:.

Recent findings suggest that responses are rendered by tts.openai, with volume and voice configurable. In my tests however tts.piper also yielded good results, and it runs entirely locally. In my tests on a RaspberryPi 5 however it added ~3-4s of latency to process the response to audio compared to tts.openai.

Since the TTS output goes to the speakers and the wake word detector listens on the microphone, the assistant plugins pause hotword detection while a conversation is active — otherwise the assistant would hear itself.

The microphone on my RPi doesn't support 16 kHz natively, so audio is captured at 44.1 kHz and software-resampled — it works, but if detection feels sluggish software resampling is usually the first suspect.

The VAD and threshold defaults were tuned on synthetic audio plus a couple of my audio recordings.

Industry observers note that different rooms, microphones and acoustics may yield different results. You may want to adjust detection_threshold on the wake word plugin and noise_floor_factor on the STT plugins if you don't feel satisfied with your mileage.

To interact via Webmentions, send an activity that references this URL from a platform that supports Webmentions, such as Lemmy, WordPress with Webmention plugins, or any IndieWeb-compatible site.

https://blog.platypush.tech/article/Rewriting-my-voice-assistant-pipeline.

It's 2026. You deserve a good local-first or local-only voice assistant on your #RaspberryPi.

#69738. Industry News: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1606 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine.
  • How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint.
  • From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

In a recent development, the emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Recent findings suggest that let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

Sources indicate that the emulator generates latest keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

Industry observers note that when it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

Recent findings suggest that how we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

Recent findings suggest that with each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an glitch in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an matter for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

Sources indicate that if you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

📅 21 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet).
  • Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.
  • According to recent reports, it's key to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

According to recent reports, it's key to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond rapidly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Sources indicate that papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:.

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:.

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:.

For each vector generation, we record:.

According to recent reports, our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 fresh features:.

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:.

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In a recent development, in our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:.

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:.

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

This gives us several useful properties:.

In a recent development, only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Industry observers note that batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:.

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:.

It has been revealed that if the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can rapidly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):.

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​.

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We at the moment use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:.

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

It has been revealed that launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:.

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

In a recent development, because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

According to recent reports, buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

According to recent reports, the revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

In a recent development, scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Sources indicate that matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

Upcoming generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Optional enhancement fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.
  • Industry observers note that A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded.
  • According to recent reports, the problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Optional enhancement fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

Industry observers note that A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

According to recent reports, the problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again.".

According to recent reports, except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored.".

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the matter affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

Industry observers note that an authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

In a recent development, microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

In a recent development, I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also upcoming ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

It has been revealed that AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

It has been revealed that headlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough reveals a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s introduces Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions.

It has been revealed that claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

It has been revealed that amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Industry observers note that optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

Sources indicate that how Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most interesting AI apps are pipelines.
  • It has been revealed that gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface.
  • Sources indicate that the best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

It has been revealed that gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

Sources indicate that the best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

👉 Try the Image Editor Pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that one graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Industry observers note that since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Sources indicate that every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

According to recent reports, decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Recent findings suggest that check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

According to recent reports, every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:.

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:.

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:.

According to recent reports, the fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:.

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

Industry News: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps.
  • The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.
  • The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

For Apple, a manufacturer that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK customers in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to customers in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

According to recent reports, without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

According to recent reports, "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

It has been revealed that "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now.".

According to recent reports, the parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a fresh order focused on British customers.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

In a recent development, A government spokesperson remarked: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies.".

Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®.

Sources indicate that true, but we're talking about Earth orbit, which isn't anywhere near a perfect vacuum. At 500 km the atmosphere is around a thousand Kelvin and any solar wind particles you run into are in the tens of thousands up to a million or so.

What you have for instance are photons from the Cosmic Background radiation, whose temperature is 2.7 K. But you also have cosmic rays, whose temperature can go into billions of degrees (Fahrenheit, Kelvin, Celsius, does not matter in this case). And because they don't interact with each other, they don't give you an average temperature.

In a recent development, that means that Space is essentially without any temperature, but that means in turn that you can't lose heat by heat exchange, because for that, you would need particle interaction. All that's left is Black Body radiation, and at temperatures around 300 K, you get a radiation of around 450 Watts per square meter of surface. And be aware that none of the surfaces should face each other and especially, all have to face away from the Sun.

Enterprise teams adopting Gemini Enterprise are increasingly building custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to connect AI agents with internal APIs, databases, and business workflows. Google Cloud Run is a natural fit for hosting these lightweight StreamableHTTP MCP servers: it scales automatically, manages TLS certificates out of the box, and integrates natively with Cloud IAM.

However, moving a custom MCP server from an initial prototype to an enterprise production environment immediately introduces three real-world security and networking challenges:.

Here is how you can solve all three challenges using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect (PSC), and FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, complete with a runnable reference implementation and setup scripts on GitHub.

Connecting Gemini Enterprise (which runs in a Google-managed tenant project) to an internal serverless Cloud Run MCP server requires bridging two network hops and one scoped DNS lookup:.

You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Recent findings suggest that why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

According to recent reports, cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:.

According to recent reports, part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

In a recent development, GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Recent findings suggest that let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because upcoming accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

Recent findings suggest that first, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

According to recent reports, the Lambda console shows the upcoming capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

According to recent reports, next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:.

According to recent reports, after pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview highlights what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I upgrade MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

Industry observers note that for production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab reveals the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

In a recent development, no GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

In a recent development, trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

It has been revealed that serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

It has been revealed that multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Looks and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

It has been revealed that large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

In a recent development, see GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Industry observers note that pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Looks and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Global consultancy PwC indicates IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.
  • It has been revealed that the Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route.

Global consultancy PwC indicates IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.

It has been revealed that the Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration.

It has been revealed that oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade.

In a recent development, thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP consumers last year found that 95 percent mentioned building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging.

Speaking to The Register, Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that.

Recent findings suggest that "Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case.".

SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw. With both of these upcoming technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems.

Sources indicate that "It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she remarked.

An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base.

Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street, building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google.

AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®.
