Breaking: The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.
  • A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve.
  • Recent findings suggest that all of that makes one number (WER) harder to game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.

Benchmarks decide what gets built. A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve. Much of the recent work on the leaderboard has gone into making the evaluation metrics more trustworthy:.

Recent findings suggest that all of that makes one number (WER) harder to game. It is still one number. A long line of work has shown that ASR error rates are not evenly distributed across the people using them. Racial disparities in automated speech recognition found commercial systems roughly twice as bad for Black speakers as for white speakers, and Quantifying Bias in Automatic Speech Recognition found further differences by gender, age and accent. None of that is visible on a leaderboard, and not because the leaderboard is hiding it. The test sets it runs on record what was said and almost nothing about who said it.

Recent findings suggest that to address this gap, we introduce two evaluation sets to the Open ASR Leaderboard: Monsoon en-IN and Monsoon hi-IN. Hindi, spoken by more than half a billion people, is the first Indic language on a multilingual tab that right now covers only European languages. Each set is released as a public split, available for self-scoring, and a private split withheld to limit benchmark-specific optimisation. The four splits are speaker-disjoint, comprising 4,888 speakers, with 12 speaker attributes recorded for each.

A test set can only expose a failure mode it varies along. Most benchmarks are built from whatever audio was readily available. Monsoon was built to vary along nine axes: geography, age, gender, vocabulary, devices, acoustic environments, speech type, speech rate, and the existence of multiple valid transcripts for the same audio. Each is a way an aggregate WER can be right on average and wrong for a particular population.

The collection method follows from that.

Four splits, two languages, collected through one pipeline.

The data is sourced from unscripted dual-channel spontaneous conversations, with clips segmented from a single channel so that each clip carries one speaker. Along with the fields reported in the table, each clip also records occupation, education, marital status, income band, handset brand, current city and years in the current district.

Five clips from the public Indian English split, with the metadata each one carries:.

29-year-old woman, West Tripura, Tripura. Student, samsung SM-G781B.

Sources indicate that 32-year-old woman, Satna, Madhya Pradesh. Unemployed, samsung SM-E146B.

22-year-old man, Rohtas, Bihar. Student, motorola moto g54 5G.

Industry observers note that 27-year-old woman, Warangal, Telangana. Unemployed, vivo V2247.

In a recent development, 57-year-old man, Puducherry. Private job, Xiaomi M2006C3LI.

According to recent reports, the English sets use standard string references, where the leaderboard's normaliser collapses most spelling variation. Hindi has far more of it, and no normaliser can resolve it, because the variants are not a fixed mapping between two conventions. The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, a list of the spellings that are accepted as correct.

Monsoon is small measured in hours and large measured in speakers. That is the design, and it is where most of the value sits.

Speaker concentration and diversity beyond the fields above.

Three properties follow, and each is a claim about variance rather than volume.

No voice carries the score: The ten largest contributors account for between 2.8% and 6.8% of total duration, and more than half of all speakers appear exactly once. A result on Monsoon is an average over hundreds of distinct voices, not a small number of talkers recorded at length. Test sets of comparable duration are usually constructed the other way.

No region or handset carries it either: The Indian English public set draws on 428 native districts across 30 states and union territories; the Hindi sets, being a Hindi-belt language, concentrate more tightly but still span 202 and 295 districts. Recordings come from 315 to 582 distinct device models, with no single model exceeding 2.1% of segments in any subset. Corpora collected on standardised hardware overfit to one microphone response; this one cannot.

In a recent development, indian English here is not one accent: This is English as it is spoken across the country, not the English of one region. All six zones are represented: in the public set, 35% of segments are contributed by southern speakers, 18% from the East, 18% from Central, 16% from the North and 11% from the West. The accent variation that follows from that spread is recorded in the metadata rather than asserted.

Monsoon ships 18 columns per segment, of which 12 are metadata, where most public ASR test sets ship an identifier, a transcript and a duration. Demographic fields are complete or near-complete; contributors consented to this use.

According to recent reports, the two languages have different geographic shapes, and the shape is informative. The Hindi sets concentrate in the Hindi belt, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for roughly 40% of speakers, which is what a Hindi corpus sampled by population should look like. The Indian English sets are much flatter: no state exceeds 13%, and a third of speakers come from outside the eight largest. Public and private halves match closely on both.

Recent findings suggest that indian state boundaries were drawn along linguistic lines, so district and state carry real accent signal, which is why these fields are released rather than summarised away. Analysis of this kind has been reported at scale for Indian ASR: district-level error rates spanning roughly 4% to 44%, with underrepresented regions well behind the Hindi belt and the metros, plus disaggregation by audio quality, speaking rate, utterance duration, gender, age and device. Those runs were on a closed benchmark. Monsoon makes the same class of analysis possible on a public leaderboard test set.

Recent findings suggest that broad geographic coverage requires recruitment across hundreds of districts rather than longer sessions from fewer speakers, and distributed recruitment at this scale introduces failure modes that a smaller collection does not face: contributors gaming the task, played-back audio submitted as live speech, and inattentive annotation. Each is addressed by an explicit check.

In a recent development, recruitment and recording: Contributors were recruited through the Voice Arena community, a global digital platform whose reach extends into the rural and semi-urban districts that speech corpora rarely cover. Pairs then recorded two-person conversations over a peer-to-peer interface, dual-channel, on assigned everyday topics. Contributors used their own handsets and their own connections. Many of those are low-end devices on unstable bandwidth, which is why that condition is present in the released audio rather than filtered out of it. Prospective contributors completed a language proficiency screening before being granted recording access, were compensated, and provided informed consent covering use in training and distribution. A per-speaker duration cap, calibrated per language to the population size and geographic distribution of its speakers, prevented a small number of prolific contributors from dominating a language or region; more than half of the speakers in these sets contribute exactly one segment.

In a recent development, elicitation: Eliciting spontaneous speech at scale presents its own difficulty, as contributors tend to produce short and sparse responses without structured guidance. Each conversation was therefore seeded with an open-ended narrative cue and progressively revealed follow-up questions, spanning domains including travel, healthcare, agriculture, education and digital services, guiding the exchange toward extended description without scripting it. Candidate topics were generated with large language models, then reviewed and localised by native-speaker linguists.

Sources indicate that quality control: Every recording passed a set of gating checks prior to transcription. The spoken language was verified against the assigned language using language identification models trained on human-annotated data across more than 30 languages. Speaker gender was confirmed against the self-reported label using a dedicated classifier, applied as corroboration of the self-report rather than as a replacement for it. A further model distinguished genuine spontaneous conversation from pre-recorded or played-back audio. Signal-to-noise ratio estimation removed recordings degraded beyond intelligibility, while natural environmental background noise was deliberately preserved so that the acoustic realism of in-the-wild speech is retained. Recordings clearing these checks were segmented by voice activity detection, split at two seconds of continuous silence or at a fifteen-second soft cap closed at the next detected silence. Segmentation was applied independently per channel, so every segment is single-speaker and single-channel. Segments then passed a DNSMOS P.808 check.

Transcription: Reference transcripts are human work. A first draft was generated by internal ASR models trained on in-domain data, none of which appear on any public leaderboard, so no system evaluated on these sets contributed to the references it is scored against. Every subsequent stage was performed by native-speaking linguists under a five-level protocol built on a strict separation of labour, in which each correction round is followed by an independent verification round performed by a different annotator, so no linguist audits their own output. A linguist first corrects the draft segment by segment against the acoustic signal; a second re-verifies it and flags residual disagreements. Subsequent levels iterate this cycle with fresh annotators, progressively resolving ambiguous phonetic realisations, code-switching boundaries, named entities, and orthographic consistency across spelling variants. Numerals are written as words, so that the transcript corresponds directly to what was spoken. Segments still flagged at the final level were returned for re-transcription before admission. Annotator behaviour was monitored automatically throughout, flagging submissions containing characters outside the target script, unnatural character or word repetitions, and unusually low or high edit counts.

What follows is one example, run on the public Indian English split, to show the kind of evaluation the metadata makes possible. It is not the finding the sets exist to deliver; it is an illustration of what becomes answerable once every clip carries a speaker.

It has been revealed that eight models on the leaderboard land between 4.81 and 4.99 WER on this set. That is 0.18 points from best to worst, inside what five hours can resolve. Ranked on the corpus, they are the same model.

According to recent reports, grouping speakers by region tells a different story. Each speaker's native district is rolled up to its zonal council, the Ministry of Home Affairs grouping of Indian states, giving five well-sampled zones. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo varies by 0.46 points across them. mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507, fourteen hundredths of a point behind it on the corpus, varies by 1.68, running 4.38 in the Central zone against 6.06 in the East. Two systems that are indistinguishable on the leaderboard differ almost fourfold in how much their accuracy depends on where the speaker is from.

Which zone is hardest is not fixed either. ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b is worst in the North, microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR-HF in the South, mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 in the East. If a single region were simply harder to transcribe, every model would rank the zones the same way. They do not, which points at the models rather than the audio.

Region is one of twelve recorded attributes, and the zones above are a coarse rollup of 428 districts. The same breakdown runs on age, education, occupation and handset, and the released files carry everything needed to reproduce it. None of it is available for a test set that records only what was said.

Sources indicate that english orthographic variation is bounded. British against American spelling, punctuation, casing, digits against words: a normaliser can map most of it to a single form, and the leaderboard's does. Hindi is not bounded in the same way. Everyday speech is heavily code-mixed, English-origin words have no settled Devanagari spelling, and compound forms are written joined or separated according to preference. A single phrase can have ten or more valid written forms, and no fixed mapping collapses them, because there is no canonical side to map to.

Industry observers note that scored with a single reference, WER rewards a system for producing the spelling the annotator happened to choose. Two systems that recognised the audio equally well can differ by several points on orthography alone.

The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, the set of written forms accepted as correct. Building it is manual work. Candidate variants are drawn from multiple ASR transcripts of the same audio and expanded with language models, then native-speaker linguists decide which are valid for that utterance and prune the rest, so only forms consistent with what was remarked are admitted.

Sources indicate that thus, for Hindi we report the Orthographically-Informed Word Error Rate (OIWER), introduced by AI4Bharat, instead of WER. A hypothesis is aligned against the accepted set at each span, so any admitted form counts as correct and only genuine recognition errors are charged.

To quantify the effect, the same hypotheses were scored twice. Flattening each lattice to its first variant per span yields a single string reference of the kind a conventional benchmark provides; any of the admitted variants would serve equally well, and a different choice would yield a different reference. Scored against the flattened reference, error rates rise for every system, and they do not rise uniformly. Rankings change as a consequence. The figure below highlights two pairs of systems that reverse order between the two references: under a single reference a system is rewarded in part for reproducing the annotator's orthography, whereas the lattice scores only recognition.

We also open source our implementation, voi-oiwer, so every result on these sets can be reproduced directly.

For the private splits, get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard and the Hugging Face team will run the evaluation. As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

In a recent development, indian-English joins the main leaderboard as Voice Arena Monsoon, in the default column set rather than as an opt-in toggle, so it contributes to the headline Average WER for every model. The private split feeds the aggregated Private (conversational) column alongside Appen and DataoceanAI data. The public and private Hindi appears in the Multilingual tab, where a model is ranked only if it supports every selected language, making that column a like-for-like comparison. Alternative, select "Hindi" from the "Language dataset breakdown" dropdown menu.

Sources indicate that hindi is a sharp case of a general problem. Any language written more than one way, spoken by people a benchmark has not sampled, carries both of the failures described here. These sets do not fix them. What they add is a way to see them: a test set on a leaderboard the field already watches, carrying enough about each speaker and each reference that a difference between two systems can be traced to who was talking and how they write it, instead of disappearing into one number.

These four sets are part of Monsoon, Voice Arena's broader dataset initiative for the Global South.

#69703. Farcall, a terminal-ready Rust PC+DOS emulator

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2809 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dialup ↗ Open Full Page

Farcall, a terminal-ready Rust PC+DOS emulator

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dialup

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, currently an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU.
  • At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt.
  • Industry observers note that coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, currently an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU. You can SSH into it and land in DOS, where you can experience fun programs including Zork, NetHack, GW-BASIC, Sopwith, and Digger Remastered.

Try it for yourself in your terminal:.

At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

Industry observers note that coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator? How hard could it be? I’d always assumed that writing an entire x86 emulator was a lot of work, but attending VCF gave me a hankering to learn more deeply how things work under the hood on computers in my vintage computing niche, but also the computers I use every day.

Industry observers note that in 1978, Intel released the 8086 chip that introduced the x86 architecture. The 1981 IBM Personal Computer used a variant, the 8088, and is the ancestor of PCs as we know them today. I picked up my very own early-model IBM PC a few years ago. It boots into PC-DOS, and runs programs off 5¼ inch floppy disks (mine has no hard drive). The Monochrome Display Adapter and the IBM 5151 monitor display its beautiful green-on-black text. The only input device is the famously clicky Model F keyboard.

An IBM PC, just like my own, that I saw recently at The National Museum of Computing in Bletchley Park, England.

Industry observers note that as a concrete target, I decided to emulate the 8088, as that’s the chip in my IBM PC. I am by far not the first person to do this—there are far more capable emulators for the IBM PC, including MartyPC, DOSBox, and 86Box. This was very much meant as a personal education mission for me.[1].

My first naive thought was that I needed to implement each of the instructions of the 8088. I knew I wanted it to boot DOS, run programs on it, and eventually boot Windows 3.1 (one of my favorite operating systems of the era). But I didn’t realize quite how much there would be to get to that point.

According to recent reports, I set out by trying to run COM files. COM is DOS’s simple executable format (you may recognize it from hits like COMMAND.COM, FORMAT.COM and indeed, WIN.COM if you ever typed “win” at the command line to start Windows). I started with a simple COM program that prints “Hello World” to the console as my first target.

My emulator, which I’m calling Farcall, started off very simply: a Rust command-line program running on my Mac, that reads in the bytes of a COM file from disk, and decodes and executes each instruction in a loop. Each instruction in the 8088 has an opcode byte (a number from 0x00 to 0xFF), optionally followed by more bytes.[2] (This is different from many RISC architectures like Arm64 where every instruction is the same width). For example:.

Farcall reads in the opcode (50, B0, or 83 above), and then however many additional bytes are necessary to interpret that type of instruction.

According to recent reports, if there were any opcodes that my emulator didn’t recognize, it would panic, and print out the unsupported opcode. I soon got into a rhythm: I would implement one instruction, run the program, and see where it next stopped. I just needed to do this ~300 more times, for each of the instruction forms.

To keep track of my todo list, I printed out the full list of instructions from Intel’s 8086 Family Users Manual, and put a blue check mark next to each instruction as I implemented it.

Sources indicate that even from my “Hello World”, I realized that it’s not enough to implement the CPU’s instructions. The x86 has an INT (interrupt) instruction that looks up an address in the interrupt vector table and calls the handler there. On the IBM PC, these handlers are typically set up by the BIOS or DOS. My “Hello World” used INT 21h to ask DOS to write a string to the screen, so in addition to implementing the CPU’s INT instruction, I had to also emulate the DOS service to write the string.

Once my Hello World COM program worked, I repeated this process a few more times with some other simple programs. And then I found out that Microsoft open-sourced some versions of MS-DOS a few years ago, so I set my sights on running MS-DOS 2.0’s MORE.COM (the pager), as my first “real” program. While it was a bit of a slog with all the instructions I had to implement, it was still an incredibly rewarding cycle–with each newly introduced instruction, the program would run just a bit more, and hundreds of instructions would fly across my screen as they were executed.

I also implemented part of INT 10h—the BIOS’s Video service, which MORE.COM uses to learn about the current screen dimensions, etc. So now I was emulating a small subset of yet another layer, the BIOS. With that, though, MORE.COM ran properly—a DOS program seemingly running in the macOS terminal.

Sources indicate that my eventual goal is to run Windows 3.1 on Farcall. However, one of the many steps before that is to get DOS to boot, since Windows 3.1 runs on top of it.

In a recent development, in order to do that, I knew that I needed to deal with boot sectors—some code at the beginning of a disk that typically loads an operating system. I own a bunch of 5¼ inch floppy disks that came with my IBM PC with software for it. I took an image of my PC-DOS 2.0 floppy, and added a “boot” mode to the emulator that would take an image and execute its boot sector, instead of a COM file.

When a PC boots from a floppy, the BIOS reads the first sector (512 bytes) into memory and executes the instructions in it. On my PC-DOS diskette, those instructions start loading DOS. Methodically, I implemented even more of the 8088’s instructions (about 200 more), and several interrupts that a BIOS would normally listen for, including keyboard support, video handling (the simplest 80x25 text mode), and reading from a floppy disk. With some persistence, I got to the point where the boot sector transferred control to the system files (IBMBIO.COM and IBMDOS.COM), and eventually to COMMAND.COM.

Getting DOS to boot was a bit of a relief—before this point my emulator was performing the work of the CPU, the BIOS, and DOS; now I could stop handling INT 21h myself and let the emulation run DOS’s real handler.

It also opened up the kinds of programs I could run. Multiplan, a spreadsheet program from 1982 (Microsoft’s answer to VisiCalc, the world’s first “killer app”) was the first one I got running, by implementing a bunch more instructions, and supporting 16-color text mode to let Multiplan's beautiful magenta-on-blue palette shine through.

So far I had been emulating a BIOS by intercepting interrupts to e.g. the Video, Keyboard, and Disk services. This was easier for me to get started, because in the emulator code I have free rein over memory and the CPU’s registers and I can talk directly to the frontend, and I can write only the specific missing pieces until things work.

Sources indicate that however, it was also limiting—the subset I’d built was just enough to boot DOS 2.0 and 3.3, but there are a lot more BIOS services, each with its own quirks and features, and the ones I had weren’t enough to boot FreeDOS, for instance. And around the same time, I discovered GLaBIOS, a modern and open-source BIOS implementation that runs on real IBM PCs.

While using someone else’s BIOS sounds easier than emulating one, it actually increased the scope of the emulator quite a bit: to support an actual BIOS ROM, you now need to emulate all the hardware the BIOS expects to talk to! This was where my naivety became clearer—I didn’t realize just how much peripheral hardware is inside an IBM PC. I knew there was a floppy drive, video card, and keyboard, of course, but I didn’t realize there’s also a Programmable Peripheral Interface (PPI), Programmable Interval Timer (PIT), and a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller.

There’s a lot I had to learn about how each of these peripherals work together. For instance, I didn’t know that the floppy disk controller works with the DMA controller to read data from a disk into memory. Thankfully, there are some great resources like the MartyPC PC Emulation Book, the datasheets for the Intel chips, and previous versions of MIT’s 6.828 course website.

I eventually implemented enough of each of these devices that I got GLaBIOS to boot. Seeing the BIOS go through its POST sequence, and then deposit me at the DOS prompt, gave me a great sense of satisfaction. And now, because the devices were actually implemented, I could focus on improving the fidelity of the graphics.

Until then, I’d only supported text output, which is all that my own IBM PC can do, since it has the Monochrome Display Adapter. But the video card can be upgraded, like to one that supports CGA, known for its iconic color palettes like magenta-cyan-white. I decided I wanted to add CGA’s graphics mode so I could run programs with color graphics.

In a recent development, to do this, I needed to convert the bytes that programs write to video memory into RGB pixels for the Farcall frontend. Quite naturally, I expected the horizontal lines of pixels, or scanlines, to be stored in order: 0, 1, 2, 3. Here’s what Sopwith looked like when I interpreted video memory that way:.

Sopwith, when reading video memory lines contiguously.

Both the monochrome and color graphics cards are built around the Motorola MC6845 chip, a Cathode Ray Tube Controller (CRTC). This controller was designed around rows of text. As it draws the screen, the CRTC outputs two numbers: a memory address that tells the card where to fetch the current character, and a scanline number to select which horizontal slice of that character to draw.

Recent findings suggest that for 320x200 graphics, IBM couldn’t simply set the CRTC to output 200 rows of one scanline each, because the register that sets the number of character rows is only 7 bits wide, so it maxes out at 127. Instead, the engineers configured it to return 100 rows of 2 scanlines each, and wired the CRTC’s two outputs to build the address at which each pixel’s data could be found in video memory.

CGA has 16 KiB of video memory, split into two 8 KiB halves. The card uses the CRTC’s memory address to select a location within one of those halves. Both scanlines in a pair use the same relative location, but the card wires the scanline number (0 or 1) to bit 13 of the final address. Because 213 = 8192, the second scanline starts 8 KiB after the first. So the first half of memory holds scanlines 0, 2, 4, and so on, and the second half holds 1, 3, 5, etc. Once the scanlines are interpreted that way, Sopwith looked correct:.

Sopwith, reading video memory correctly with 8 KiB offset.

Industry observers note that I started Farcall as a terminal program that could run COM files in my macOS terminal. There was something attractive about seeing an old DOS program running in a modern terminal, as opposed to in a graphical window like a normal VM hypervisor.

Recent findings suggest that this worked great for text-mode programs, but I wanted to go further to see if I could render CGA graphics-mode programs directly in the terminal too. I learned that the terminal emulator I use, Ghostty, supports the Kitty graphics protocol, which allows terminal applications to display inline images. I figured I could try using this to stream each frame from the guest’s video memory. And it turns out this works—though it feels like it’s at the edge of what the protocol and Ghostty’s implementation are meant to support. (e.g. I found I could reliably crash Ghostty when sending zlib frames, and a change in a recent version of Ghostty made frames flicker).

Now that I could display graphics-mode programs like Sopwith in the terminal, I wanted to share this experience of “running DOS in your terminal” with others, so I decided to put an installation of my emulator on a public SSH server. An increasing number of iconic DOS programs of the era are now being made open source by their owners (including MS-DOS itself as I mentioned, but also programs like GW-BASIC, Zork, and Sopwith), so I decided to put those in the environment for anyone to try.

As I was preparing to launch the SSH service, one concern I needed to solve was that of performance. Even though I was emulating a processor operating at 4.77 MHz on a VPS with a shared CPU supposedly running at 2.4 GHz, I was only able to fit 6 or so instances of Farcall running Sopwith per core before the emulation started dropping frames.

According to recent reports, there were a couple things that were contributing to unnecessary CPU usage. Firstly, before every step of the emulation, I was checking the clock to see if it was time to pause emulation and handle some input/draw the screen. In profiling the code using a sample program, I found that fetching monotonic time (Instant::now() in Rust) was actually using ~43% of CPU time. Making the loop only check every 128 steps removed this bottleneck. (Note that this didn’t change the fact that the emulator is nowhere near cycle-accurate, or properly emulating how long each instruction or hardware operation takes; I’m pretending that every instruction takes equal time, for example).

Sources indicate that another culprit was in my Kitty graphics code. Each frame is sent down as a separate PNG image.[3] At first I was sending full-color RGB PNGs, which was contributing to a significant amount of CPU usage in preparing each frame. However, by switching to 4-bit indexed (palette) images (which works perfectly given that you can only use one of 16 colors in CGA in normal circumstances[4]), I was able to save more than 70% of CPU time in preparing the frames.

I was surprised just how much I’ve learned from this project in such a short period of time. I’ve been using computers since the 90s and am familiar with words like IRQs, DMA, and Cylinders/Heads/Sectors—but it wasn’t until I had to implement them in software that I truly appreciated them for what they are. It was also a fantastic refresher for how CPUs work at the instruction level, which feels a lot more concrete now. On the other hand, I was not ready for how promptly “emulating a CPU” ballooned into “emulating a whole computer including all its peripherals”.

As for what’s next: My emulator is far from complete, and I still have a goal of running Windows 3.1. Probably the biggest hurdle in the way is support for protected mode, and emulating a 286. (Windows 3.0 is easier to run in this regard, since it supports the 8088, and still supported real mode). Even before that, I need to support hard drives, as well as a newer graphics mode like EGA or VGA. There’s a lot to do—but I look forward to learning a lot more about how computers work along the way!

In a recent development, you can try out Farcall yourself on a standard SSH client. You will unlock the full graphical experience on terminal emulators that support Kitty graphics like Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, and Konsole.

At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

The source code is licensed under the MIT license and is available at https://github.com/keito/farcall. Provenance of the programs on the SSH server is available here.

Recent findings suggest that I wrote the code for the emulator by hand. I used Codex to help write unit tests and some test programs, and perform research. ↩.

An opcode is optionally preceded by one or more prefixes, which can do things like repeat the instruction. ↩.

I initially sent zlib-compressed pixels, but it kept crashing Ghostty, caused by a bug in the Zig DEFLATE library, so I switched to sending PNG images. This bug is fixed in the latest Ghostty after they switched to Wuffs. ↩.

Sources indicate that without some cool shenanigans. ↩.

Dutch data watchdog highlights safety complications with AI glasses

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Devices found to misinterpret medication instructions and other scenarios impacting human safety.
  • The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.
  • The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring complications, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Devices found to misinterpret medication instructions and other scenarios impacting human safety.

The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring complications, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.

Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role.".

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.

It has been revealed that "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," mentioned Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP.

Industry observers note that "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot right now be justified.".

It has been revealed that the warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.

The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests indicated that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that customers were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.

Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”.

Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable.

The AP stated that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.

"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them.

However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to owners and bystanders.".

Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.

"It is vital that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said.

According to recent reports, "Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is vital that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience.".

When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.

"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," stated Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.

Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone owners have slowly eradicated that over time.

Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.

On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones.

However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.

A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.

There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy.

A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

Industry observers note that the two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®.

#69701. Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1603 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible.
  • Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.
  • The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution aims, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations.

Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.

The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub.

According to recent reports, we are also launching Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware.

A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them.

According to recent reports, portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features.

In a recent development, this is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. Higher-level runtimes can only be as efficient as the operations they dispatch. By making those operations individually discoverable, testable, benchmarkable, and versioned, we can improve the foundation independently while keeping a stable contract for the layers above it.

It has been revealed that each kernel in the collection has its own repository and kernel card. The card documents the operation's semantics, inputs, outputs, attributes, supported data types, source files, and a ready-to-run @huggingface/kernels example.

According to recent reports, for example, ai.onnx.Add implements elementwise addition with multidirectional broadcasting. It is one of the simplest operations in a neural network, used everywhere from residual connections to adding a bias. Its card documents the two inputs, the broadcasted output shape, supported data types, and the variants available for different shapes and devices.

Behind the card, the repository contains the artifacts needed to understand and evaluate the implementation:.

In a recent development, this structure turns a shader into a reusable software artifact. The interface is inspectable without reading WGSL, correctness and performance cases travel with the implementation, and published versions can be loaded explicitly rather than depending on an unversioned file URL. Our kernels can also serve as reference implementations for developers building custom WebGPU kernels or integrating these operations into their own runtimes.

It has been revealed that running these kernels requires a browser with WebGPU support. WebGPU availability depends on the browser, operating system, GPU, and driver. You can check for it in JavaScript with "gpu" in navigator.

@huggingface/kernels provides the bridge between a kernel repository and your application. Call getKernel with a Hub repository ID and a contract version, then invoke the returned function with typed input data and tensor shapes. Here is a small bias-add example:.

Sources indicate that the second input is broadcast across the first dimension, producing an output with shape [2, 3]. The loader derives that output shape and logical data type from the manifest contract and the inputs, then allocates c automatically.

Addition on six floats is deliberately the smallest possible demo. At this size, the GPU round trip costs far more than the math. The point is the call pattern: it stays exactly the same for the heavyweight operations where optimized kernels actually pay off, such as matrix multiplication (ai.onnx.MatMul). Only the repository ID and the inputs change.

Even this elementary operation illustrates why kernels need variants. Equal-shape addition can use a direct vectorized path, while broadcasted inputs need different indexing logic. The published Add kernel includes variants for equal shapes, vectorized broadcasting, scalar processing, and general broadcasting. The runtime can select an implementation that fits the current call and device without changing the application-facing API.

The version: 1 option selects version 1 of the published kernel contract. It is separate from an ONNX opset, an operator's since_version, or a model revision. Keeping those concepts separate lets applications depend on a stable JavaScript-facing contract while kernel implementations evolve behind it.

So, how much of a difference do optimized kernels actually make? We put our collection head-to-head with ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU, using ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0-dev.20260826-b1f76d586a. We started with 1,756 test cases across all 207 operations and kept the 809 cases where both sides produced matching outputs and reliable timings.

Industry observers note that across those comparisons, our kernels were 2.57x faster by geometric mean and 1.90x faster at the median, with 629 wins, 176 losses, and 4 ties. Here is a closer look at four familiar operations:.

Sources indicate that some individual wins were much bigger. A particularly difficult bilinear Einsum case (i,ij,j with size 4096) ran in 0.136 ms with our kernel versus 1,396 ms with ORT WebGPU: more than 10,000x faster. A row-wise CumSum over [256, 4096] was 301x faster, at 0.016 ms versus 4.784 ms. These are unusual cases rather than the speedups you should expect everywhere, but they show how much a specialized kernel can help when a general implementation hits a slow path.

It has been revealed that we timed the work done on the GPU itself, leaving out setup such as loading kernels, creating sessions, uploading inputs, compiling shaders, and reading outputs back. Very short workloads are naturally harder to measure, and small cases can benefit from the GPU cache, so these numbers are best read as a useful comparison rather than a promise for every application.

They are also results for individual operations, not complete models. Exact performance will change across GPUs and browsers, which is why Fleet is so crucial for building a broader picture.

We are also working with the ONNX Runtime team to upstream these improvements so they can benefit the broader ONNX Runtime Web ecosystem.

Sources indicate that webGPU performance varies across GPUs, browsers, and drivers, so results from one machine only tell part of the story. Fleet lets anyone run correctness and performance checks in the browser and see how the kernels behave on their hardware.

Recent findings suggest that with consent, each run privately contributes evidence that helps us spot device-specific failures, compare variants, and improve selection rules. The goal is simple: use broad, real-world coverage to make the kernels faster and more reliable for everyone.

According to recent reports, the initial 207 kernels are a starting point, not the end state. Publishing kernels independently on the Hub gives us a common place to inspect contracts, compare implementations, reproduce correctness checks, and improve performance without embedding every shader directly into every runtime.

The collection is also part of the Hub's broader kernel ecosystem: on the Kernels page, the WebGPU kernels sit alongside kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and other platforms, and can be filtered, sorted, and explored like any other artifact on the Hub.

The pieces reinforce one another:.

This is the low-level foundation for the next steps in our browser inference stack. We are excited to connect these kernels to higher-level model tooling, continue expanding operation coverage, and make fast local inference easier to use across the WebAI ecosystem.

Explore the WebGPU kernel collection, try @huggingface/kernels, and join the Fleet to contribute evidence from your device and help us make the kernels better for everyone.

The Fleet part may matter as much as the kernels. The 809 comparable cases on an M4 are useful, but browser, driver and device variance is where WebGPU tends to get painful. Will Fleet eventually expose per-device distributions, or is the proposal to use the runs only for aggregate selection rules?

In an automated build system, I could see per device kernels, made more interesting by fusion of ops.

The area that obviously needs more attention are the 947 tests that did not result in reliable output. This could be the test, it could be that the ORT WebGPU is wrong, or the new kernel is wrong, or the test harness had complications, hard to know from the outside. Perhaps the Fleet thing is meant to improve this.

Very excited to see such attention at making WebGPU first class in ML!

@sroussey Agreed—the excluded 947 need a taxonomy before the 2.57× summary can travel. I'd want counts by operation and device for unsupported, ORT mismatch, latest-kernel mismatch, and harness/timeout, with raw failing cases downloadable. Then Fleet can optimize only within a proven-correct compatibility envelope; fusion and per-device tuning become much safer.

It has been revealed that excellent! This will help our WebAI community continue developing highly optimized solutions. Many thanks @Xenova and @nico-martin for the great work you have been doing.

GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • It has been revealed that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • Sources indicate that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

It has been revealed that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

Sources indicate that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

Sources indicate that that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

Sources indicate that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

According to recent reports, we removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in people. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

Industry observers note that A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Recent findings suggest that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or concerns, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Recent findings suggest that web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

It has been revealed that during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One latest machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, newly introduced commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, upcoming connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

According to recent reports, we took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the concern.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

It has been revealed that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Problems, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

Recent findings suggest that A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

Industry observers note that the pool was already running near capacity when some enhancement requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

#69698. BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1421 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.
  • Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a latest method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.
  • Recent findings suggest that A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.

Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a latest method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.

Recent findings suggest that A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following. But the individual tasks inside it may depend on more than that stated goal. Take BBQ, a benchmark designed to test whether models rely on social stereotypes. One question asks about a grandson and grandfather trying to book an Uber. It probes age bias, but also requires the model to track who’s who and reason from the evidence provided rather than assumptions.

According to recent reports, and even within a single benchmark, different groups of questions and tasks can measure different things. WildJailbreak, for example, includes harmful jailbreak prompts alongside benign prompts designed to test whether a model refuses harmless requests too often. The harmful prompts are more closely associated with safety, while the benign prompts are more closely associated with general reasoning. Averaging them into a single benchmark score can obscure that difference.

Recent findings suggest that benchMIRT helps researchers separate those signals and see what’s actually driving a benchmark’s score. It does this by analyzing how models perform on each question or task and estimating which underlying capabilities are most closely associated with getting it right.

BenchMIRT takes cues from Item Response Theory (IRT), a technique originating in psychometrics—the field concerned with measuring abilities and traits from patterns of test responses. IRT starts from a simple idea: not every question tells you the same amount about the person taking a test. Some are harder than others, and some do a better job of distinguishing stronger performers from weaker ones.

Researchers have previously applied single-dimensional IRT to individual benchmarks, including in our Fluid Benchmarking work. BenchMIRT extends that approach with multidimensional IRT, or MIRT, allowing it to separate multiple capabilities that may contribute to performance on the same questions.

It has been revealed that benchMIRT applies IRT at both the model and question level. For a given model, it estimates the model’s strength on the capabilities reflected across the selected benchmarks. For each question, it estimates how difficult the question is and how well it distinguishes models that are stronger or weaker on those capabilities.

We trained BenchMIRT on benchmarking results from 100 LLMs across 16 benchmarks and more than 34K questions. Six of those benchmarks measure general reasoning, including MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MATH, and BBH. The other 10 come from our Olmo 3 safety suite, including HarmBench, StrongReject, WildJailbreak, BBQ, WMDP, and XSTest.

Crucially, we didn’t tell BenchMIRT which benchmarks were measuring which capabilities. It independently recovered two dominant dimensions: safety and general reasoning. When we repeated our analysis from scratch, those same two dimensions emerged each time, suggesting the result was stable rather than specific to one analysis.

For many benchmarks, BenchMIRT largely confirmed their intended focus: strong performance on reasoning benchmarks tracked with reasoning ability, while strong performance on jailbreak and harmful-content benchmarks tracked with safety.

But BenchMIRT also revealed a more complicated picture in some evaluations.

It has been revealed that BBQ, which evaluates social bias and is commonly grouped with safety benchmarks, aligned much more strongly with general reasoning in BenchMIRT’s analysis. That means a low BBQ score may partly reflect difficulty understanding or reasoning through certain questions, rather than safety behavior alone.

Recent findings suggest that WMDP behaves differently from most safety benchmarks. It tests dangerous dual-use knowledge in areas such as biology, chemistry, and cybersecurity—for example, knowledge that could help someone misuse a biological agent or exploit a computer system. BenchMIRT found that WMDP scores were more strongly associated with general reasoning than with safety. Stronger general reasoning, however, was associated with lower WMDP scores, because the benchmark counts refusing or failing to provide the dangerous knowledge as the desired response.

It has been revealed that these findings don’t necessarily mean the benchmarks are flawed or incomplete. Rather, they show that a single benchmark score can combine several different signals—and that BenchMIRT can help disentangle those signals and make the score easier to interpret.

Sources indicate that item difficulty and discrimination in both dimensions for Harmbench. Dimension 0 models the safety dimension, while Dimension 1 maps to the general reasoning dimension.

In a recent development, bar size and direction show the Pearson correlation, across 100 open-weight LLMs, between BenchMIRT ability scores and benchmark scores on a −1 to 1 scale—pink for general reasoning and teal for safety; bars extending left of center are negative. Bold with underline marks each row’s stronger correlation, except where the two are too close to separate; asterisks mark p < 0.01.

BenchMIRT can also help identify which questions in an evaluation are most informative about the capability the benchmark is trying to measure.

Using BenchMIRT’s question-level estimates, we ranked questions across the same 16 benchmarks used to train BenchMIRT and kept those that did the best job of distinguishing stronger from weaker models, while still preserving a mix of easier and harder questions.

Recent findings suggest that across those benchmarks, keeping only 10% of the questions generally preserved nearly the same picture of which models were stronger or weaker on the underlying safety or reasoning capability as using the full set. Keeping 50% of the questions often matched the full benchmark’s measure of those capabilities even more closely.

In a recent development, benchMIRT can also use the patterns it learns across models and questions to predict how a model would perform on a benchmark question it hasn’t been observed answering. In our experiments, it correctly predicted whether a model would answer a held-out question correctly 79% of the time. By comparison, a simpler approach that assumes a model will perform on each question about as well as it does on the benchmark overall was correct 70% of the time.

In practice, that means BenchMIRT can estimate model performance more precisely from what it has already learned about the model’s abilities and the demands of each question, without needing to evaluate every model on every question.

BenchMIRT offers a way to better understand and refine the benchmarks researchers use to evaluate model capabilities. By looking at individual questions rather than only overall scores, it can reveal when a benchmark mixes together different capabilities, identify clusters of questions that behave differently from the rest, and surface questions that add little useful information about the capability the benchmark is meant to measure.

In a recent development, there are vital limitations. The models we used to train and evaluate BenchMIRT were all released by March 2025, so our analysis doesn’t capture how BenchMIRT behaves on newer generations of LLMs. And the dimensions BenchMIRT discovers depend on the benchmark set it’s given—safety and reasoning emerged as the dominant dimensions across the 16 benchmarks we selected for this project, but a different mix of evaluations could surface different underlying capabilities.

In a recent development, there are trade-offs, too. If the goal is to rank models by their predicted performance on randomly held-out items, the benchmark’s average score performs slightly better than BenchMIRT. BenchMIRT’s advantage is the finer-grained picture it provides of performance on individual questions.

That question-level detail can also cut both ways: the same estimates that help identify a benchmark’s most informative safety questions could be used to remove them, producing a weaker evaluation that an unsafe model could pass. Existing tools already make it possible to trim evaluations in similar ways, and we think the added transparency into what benchmark questions are actually measuring is worth that risk—but it’s a real one.

It has been revealed that still, we see BenchMIRT – and future tools like it – as a step toward more targeted benchmark design and efficient evaluation. By showing which questions are actually driving a benchmark’s results, these approaches could help researchers build evaluations that are smaller, more focused, and easier to interpret, while giving a clearer picture of the capabilities they’re meant to measure.

Good read! Reliable evaluation is essential for understanding how well AI systems perform and where they need improvement. Benchmarking and systematic testing can help developers make better decisions about model selection, application quality, and readiness for real-world use. In Generative AI app development, these practices are particularly useful for identifying limitations before expanding access or introducing additional features.
