Latest Update: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 'Agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction,' Amazon CISO said.
  • Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.
  • The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

'Agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction,' Amazon CISO said.

Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance.

According to recent reports, in this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory.

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register.

The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.

"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.

Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

According to recent reports, "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.".

Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

In a recent development, this campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.

"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

In a recent development, linkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.

Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

LinkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the organization moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.

Industry observers note that linkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.

According to recent reports, with Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.

Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,.

Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.

Industry observers note that the deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.

LinkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The manufacturer also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.

The converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bertptrs

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that after some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself.
  • In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.
  • Sources indicate that in theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.

Sources indicate that in theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its important work. For example:.

Industry observers note that the following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError), which will trigger a panic when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

You might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this is the common case.

I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she works on lend themselves more towards these challenges compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

This section is only tangentially related to the topic at hand, but I already wrote it and wasn’t ready to kill my darlings.1 Skip to the next section to continue the discussion on poisoning.

Recent findings suggest that in Rust, for most platforms, mutexes are implemented using the futex2 system call. It allows for operations to remain purely in user-space as long as the mutex in question isn’t contended, which is nice for performance reasons.

Under the hood, a mutex is a simple 32-bit integer on most platforms even though it only holds three unique values:.

Flow chart showing how a mutex acquisition is implemented in Rust, using atomic operations and futex primitives. Note how the uncontended case remains entirely in user-space and does not sleep the thread.

Recent findings suggest that rust implements this with a few atomic operations and the futex_wait call. Crucially, the path for locking a mutex that isn’t contended is a single atomic operation. The only operation that requires a context switch is futex_wait.

Industry observers note that unlocking is even simpler. The thread that holds the mutex first releases the lock, then optionally, if there was an indication that the lock was contended, wakes any sleeping threads so they can try to acquire the lock.

Flow chart showing how a mutex release in Rust. First, we swap the current value with 0, and depending on whether it was originally 1 (simply locked) or 2 (contended), we optionally wake any sleeping threads.

According to recent reports, as discussed in too much detail above, (un)locking mutexes is cheap as long as they’re not contended, and when contended, they are at least cheap instruction wise. This is where poisoning mutexes get you.

In short, being able to poison is a cost that is always paid, but seldom used. To start, poisoning is essentially implemented by adding an AtomicBool field to every Mutex. Due to alignment, this grows the size of every mutex by anywhere from zero bytes to an additional pointer. This isn’t terrible but for use cases where you have many mutexes guarding small objects, this can add up.

Industry observers note that the real glitch to me however is in code size. Let’s start with another contrived example, a function that reads its argument, copies it, and returns it. An idealised version of that would be the following.

According to recent reports, this compiles down to 2 instructions and a label. Copy the data into the register then return.

Industry observers note that of course, this doesn’t work for any context that needs shared mutation, but we can consider it our baseline. Perfection would look like this. So, let’s ignore that atomic integers exist and add a mutex to this story. We will go over the generated assembly code for each, and you can compare the code in its entirety in this Compiler Explorer overview.

We can patch the code above to actually use mutexes, and simply lock-then-unwrap the mutex.

This compiles to a total of 147 lines of assembly which I’m not going to reproduce here in full.

To divide that up a different way, we have.

Recent findings suggest that most of this is inlined into the function. This in turn affects performance, as this limits how much of your “real” code fits in the CPU’s instruction cache. The laptop I’m writing this on has a paltry 32KiB of instruction cache. Luckily we can do better.

In a recent development, most of the code generated in the previous example had to do with setting up the panic, and checking the conditions. But we don’t care about panicking. We can simply acknowledge the PoisonError and continue. That looks as follows:.

This results in only 68 lines of assembly, which is much better, though all of it is inlined to our function. Compared to before, we’ve lost all panic related code. There’s still some unnecessary branching related to whether the mutex is poisoned, as well as a little dance to track poisoning in our function. Our function can never panic, but compiler optimisations currently do not remove the atomic loads and stores involved here. Nevertheless, if you want to target stable Rust and you don’t care about panics, this is what you should do at the moment.

Recent findings suggest that in the current nightly builds of Rust, there are non-poisoning mutexes that can don’t have any of the overhead. We can optimise our code from above to make use of them.

No unwrapping, and it only results in 34 lines of assembly code. This is short enough for me to walk through it.

I’ve added comments and labels to the assembly so the steps from the (un)locking flow charts become visible. As far as assembly code goes, it’s very readable and simple. Which, of course, is exactly what you want from fundamental library code.

The additional logic checking the poison state, adding a destructor for the mutex guard, and, if you choose ergonomics, even panic machinery, significantly bloats the code of a rather fundamental operation.

Industry observers note that besides the purely technical argument that poisoning makes all code larger and slower than it needs to be, there is a different one. As discussed previously, code that doesn’t care about mutex poisoning should generally write:.

Sources indicate that it’s reasonably efficient and available on stable Rust. But that whole unwrap_or_else part takes up more than half the line. No worry, you might say, we can make it shorter:.

This works well enough. It’s less efficient than the previous example, but it’s nice and short. If your code never panics, it’s even perfectly safe. You might have spotted a load-bearing “if” already. It’s kind of hard to guarantee your code does not panic. Array indexing, integer division, and a whole host of other features might panic unexpectedly.

Industry observers note that this is hard for experienced developers, but for those learning it’s even worse. It also trains bad habits. Every time a beginner Rust developer writes unwrap() instead of handling their errors, a puppy steps on a Lego brick. Or causes a widespread internet outage. One of the two, I forget which.

We should not want to include APIs into the standard library that return a Result that is “expected” to be unwrapped. Infallible operations should not fail.

Poisoning protects against a task panicking in the middle of an invariant violation. But why must this be specific to mutexes? The example from before works just as well with a simple mutable borrow. Panics may still happen, and you may still catch them.

In a recent development, this is actually a fairly common problem. In a more recent blog post, researchers at Microsoft highlight various places they’ve found where even the standard library gets this wrong.

Recent findings suggest that in most cases however, this is fine, as it is with the mutex example given in the beginning. You don’t need to poison this reference. But for applications where you do, it’s kinda nice to be able to.

It’s not hard to imagine a wrapper that adds poisoning behaviour when you want to have it. Crucially, this needs to be an additive wrapper. You can add a poisoning system to something. You cannot strip out the poisoning system from a primitive that has it. Poison safety is important for the specific use cases that need it, but most do not.

I don’t believe it’s worth it to saddle mutexes in particular with this overhead when the problem is near universal with any mutable state. State invariants are just hard that way.

Sources indicate that one might draw a comparison between poison safety and buffer safety. In Rust, we always do bounds checking, relying on the compiler to optimise it out in cases it can be proven redundant. Can’t poison safety be the same? And the answer, it turns out, is no.

The compiler cannot optimise poisoning away. It requires any mutex carry additional data to track it. Maybe the compiler can figure out one particular critical section cannot panic, and therefore it can leave out the setup and clean-up, but in general it cannot avoid checking the state. This is overhead that always applies, and hurts, especially in environments where code size is more restricted.

In C++, there are a few choices in the standard that make certain containers less efficient than they could be4. Because of how standardisation works, the containers can never be “fixed”. This causes third party implementations, such as Abseil and Boost, to become the de facto standard.

Mutexes in Rust suffer from the same problem. The standard library has poisoning, but people don’t want poisoning, so instead they opt for crates like parking_lot. I believe this is bad for the ecosystem as a whole. When the standard library offers a feature, it should be an uncontroversially good choice, unless you are doing something hyper specific. We don’t have to be “batteries included” but the parts that are there should be a good fit.

Rain’s blog argued for option 1. I believe we both agree that option 2 is a terrible idea. I think we should do at least option 3. Option 4 would be a good edition improvement, but it is also a significant compatibility glitch, and even I find it hard to argue that it’s really worth it.

Which is a roundabout way of saying that we really should stabilise std::sync::nonpoison and definitely should not make std::sync::Mutex panic by default.

According to recent reports, it is becoming apparent to me that I just like explaining mutexes and I don’t know what to do about that. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that fast Userspace muTEX. See futex(2) for more on the system call and futex(7) for its semantics ↩︎.

According to recent reports, for generic definitions (e.g. Mutex) the compiler must generate code for every unique T that gets used, and for loads of reasons often more than once per T. The compiler development docs have a deeper explanation of monomorphisation. ↩︎.

A famous example is std::unordered_map, which suffers from being over-specified and that prevents more efficient implementations. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, on 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

In a recent development, the video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

Recent findings suggest that in this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:.

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:.

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

Industry observers note that I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The newly introduced material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

Recent findings suggest that the paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a substantial part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

According to recent reports, this project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

Recent findings suggest that in that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Industry observers note that most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:.

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Recent findings suggest that those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:.

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I debuted the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Recent findings suggest that disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

Industry observers note that the library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Industry observers note that note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

According to recent reports, his blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a major pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

The gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

Industry observers note that the pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

The tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

According to recent reports, no human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

In a recent development, if we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Recent findings suggest that before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

In a recent development, another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:.

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

Sources indicate that with that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were introduced for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:.

Recent findings suggest that the three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

According to recent reports, the pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

According to recent reports, this is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, highlights almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

What the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

Sources indicate that the paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

It has been revealed that since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs released with it have been running clean since.

It has been revealed that the reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

The rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Industry observers note that multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

In a recent development, and underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:.

The rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

In a recent development, the per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

Sources indicate that the method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

Nvidia’s journey to forge the one CPU SKU to rule them all

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of newly introduced SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between.
  • According to recent reports, but if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill.
  • Nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of newly introduced SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between.

According to recent reports, but if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill. “There was sort of an overskewing, for many years on the other vendors side of things,” he told El Reg on the sidelines of Supercomputing 2026 this week.

Nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space. The company’s first part, called Grace, debuted in 2023, but didn’t see widespread deployment outside AI headnodes, high-end NICs, and a handful of standalone CPU deployments by hyperscalers like Meta.

We explored the chip in greater detail earlier this year, but the GPU slinger’s latest CPU, Vera, is a different beast. In addition to showing up as part of Nvidia’s Vera-Rubin superchips, the CPU will also be offered in standalone CPU racks, storage, and context memory systems. Just this week, Nvidia announced a new rack with 192 Vera CPUs aimed at high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, which don’t translate well to GPUs. And at least on paper, a single SKU with 88 cores clocking to 3.3 GHz powers all of them.

Historically, CPUs with different combinations of cores, clocks, I/O, and power have been used in these roles.

Recent findings suggest that according to Finder, most datacenter CPUs haven’t been loaded that heavily, and as a result unloaded latency has been the optimization point. As a consequence, CPUs that rely on high core counts to boost throughput often suffer from elevated loaded latencies.

Recent findings suggest that on the flip side, chipmakers can optimize for loaded latency, but this usually comes at the expense of throughput. We see this pretty clearly across AMD’s last few generations of Epycs, where it designed both space-efficient Zen-C cores that prioritize throughput and fatter frequency-optimized versions that prioritize latency.

“As more cores are up and running, your latency to memory gets higher because you have to deal with congestion on the connectivity buses,” More than Moore analyst Ian Cutress tells The Reg. “What Nvidia is saying is right. Sometimes, you do have to pick between core count and core latency.”.

88 custom cores, 176 funky threads, 1.5 TB of laptop RAM, and 1.8 TB/s of NVLink connectivity — this isn't your typical datacenter chip.

Industry observers note that with Vera, Nvidia sought to thread that needle to design a balanced architecture that maintains low latencies and high throughput even when all 88 cores are loaded. This does mean making some compromises – in particular, the CPU's vector unit isn’t the beefiest. But if you’ve got GPUs capable of running vectorized code, that compromise starts to make a lot more sense – and if you’re buying Vera you almost certainly do.

“If you do a few things like that, you can actually get a part that, for the workloads people care about — knowledge agents for CI/CD, for software engineering, or databases and analytics — you can build a part that gets you the same performance per core as the frequency-optimized x86 parts at the same throughput per watt as the density-optimized parts,” Finder argued.

We should note that Nvidia isn’t unique in this line of thinking. Cloud providers have long passed on the highest core-count parts in Intel or AMD’s lineup in favor of parts they feel deliver the right mix of throughput, latency, memory bandwidth, and capacity.

According to recent reports, the reason, in part, is that cloud providers don’t know exactly what their customers will actually be doing with those cores, and so it’s better to offer something that’s well-rounded than one that has the highest clocks or lowest latency. This same logic works pretty well for agent sandboxes.

“Nvidia is confident that it understands the market well enough that one chip will cover most use cases,” Cutress remarked. “You could argue that Nvidia just wants to corner that bulk market.”.

Having mentioned that, there are plenty of reasons to have multiple SKUs or product lines. Throughout much of AMD’s latest launch cycle, the House of Zen has argued its chips make for better agentic CPUs because agents aren’t one workload but many. Some may benefit from higher core counts while others may benefit from higher frequency, and AMD’s more diverse portfolio offers choice.

Sources indicate that to that point, Vera does have one trick up its sleeve: a split personality. The processor is one of the few Arm chips that supports simultaneous multithreading (SMT), but the way it works differs wildly from what Intel would call Hyperthreading.

Sources indicate that when enabled, SMT effectively bifurcates Vera’s Olympus cores. Eighty-eight cores turns into something that functionally looks more like 176 narrower cores. So if you need more throughput than 88 cores afford, or your workload doesn’t benefit materially from a wider core, Vera does offer some flexibility.

In a recent development, 16 channels of DDR5, 5 GHz clock speeds, and support for CXL 3.1 memory god boxes? What's not to like?

Industry observers note that A broader SKU stack also helps with binning. Chip manufacturing isn’t a perfect process, and you’re going to run into defective cores from time to time. Binning allows chipmakers to sell these defective chips at a discount.

Cutress suspects that Nvidia is probably doing this for its customers and it’s just not advertising them as different SKUs the way Intel and AMD have the past few decades.

For instance, a hyperscaler might be happy to take a 72-core variant of Vera that clocks a little higher or delivers more memory bandwidth per core for the same amount of power.

Recent findings suggest that but for now we have just the one, for the green lord on their green throne in the land of AI where the bots lie. ®.

  • Zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category.

In a recent development, zellij is a relatively latest entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

Zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives owners the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Sources indicate that earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each latest agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the latest one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:.

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

Industry observers note that the bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

According to recent reports, before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

Sources indicate that or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

Industry observers note that funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

Recent findings suggest that A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent states so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

Industry observers note that published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

Sources indicate that A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

It has been revealed that compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

Sources indicate that the lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

According to recent reports, ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Recent findings suggest that full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

Industry observers note that longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls.
  • Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.
  • Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls.

Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.

Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.

"Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.".

The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private.

Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text.

Whittaker claims that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents.

Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system.

"We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said.

"Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are right now unable to implement these protections on macOS.".

Industry observers note that apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately.

Sources indicate that with macOS 27.3, right now in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs.

Sources indicate that "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring people clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.".

Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers.

While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri demonstrates that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome.

AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants.

According to recent reports, amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others.

Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few.

In a recent development, the web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy.

Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®.

We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Violetpixel

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit.
  • When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are.
  • The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST.

Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:.

Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.

Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365, Air Traffic Control, United Airlines' systems, the NSA's network, many major banks, Apple's systems, and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

I guess that depends on how you look at it.

I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics.

Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this.

It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real.

In a recent development, thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system).

We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a major problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail.

It has been revealed that I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now.

Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.
