📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

It has been revealed that discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently revealed rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project (codenamed Phoenix) eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.

Vishnevskiy expanded on the rewrite on X:.

In a recent development, we’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with people soon™. (And it’s not Tauri, it’s GPUI, so good guess everyone.).

According to recent reports, the desktop app thus drops Chromium/Node.js for GPUI, the open-source, GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework built by the Zed team for the Zed editor. Zed is an open-source code editor written in Rust for macOS, Linux, and Windows by a team including the creators of GitHub’s Atom code editor, which was sunsetted in 2022, four years after Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub. Zed touts a narrow focus on performance and user (i.e., developer) experience:.

VS Code won by being good enough for everyone. Zed wins by being excellent for developers who refuse to compromise on speed.

Discord’s mobile app rewrite drops React Native, instead directly leveraging native iOS and Android views and reusing a common Rust core.

Industry observers note that the browser client keeps rendering HTML with the application logic layer compiled to WebAssembly. Embedded web surfaces (e.g., YouTube videos and Activities), however, invoke an OS webview, with Electron’s built-in browser no longer available.

Vishnevskiy signals decreasing RAM usage, startup time, and latency as key motivations behind the rewrite:.

In a recent development, the upcoming Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time.

Early internal builds for the desktop app reveal RAM usage at around 290 MB (measured with two accounts logged in simultaneously) and a near-instant cold start versus 5.5 s on Electron.

Vishnevskiy showcased similar improvements on mobile with a load time under 2 seconds for the rewrite versus approximately 5 seconds for the legacy app.

Sources indicate that elias Floreteng, in his master’s thesis at KTH this year (An Empirical Study of React Native’s Latest Architecture), reported performance gains across several metrics for native Swift and Kotlin over React Native, even with its new architecture. The controlled benchmark involves a 1,000-row scrollable image list using stock list and image components, with identical assets and row geometry across all binaries. Floreteng concludes that Swift beats React Native across every comparable runtime metric on iOS. On Android, the gap to native is small and runs in both directions, with native ahead on memory and CPU.

On desktop, Zed proved that leveraging GPUI could provide better performance over Electron and alternative frameworks reusing the device’s native webview (e.g., Tauri).

While Tauri also uses a Rust backend, it leverages the operating system’s native webview. This has the advantage of letting web developers reuse their knowledge of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while also avoiding the bundling of Chromium. Executable size is, as a result, generally smaller. Tauri apps’ RAM usage on Windows, however, tends to be similar to that of their Electron counterparts, as the same core, resource-hungry browser technology is used. Webview behavior may also be inconsistent across operating systems.

GPUI replaces the browser engine with a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework that targets 120-frames-per-second rendering without garbage-collection pauses. In exchange for the reported performance gains, developers give up many rendering and accessibility features that come baked into the browser (e.g., text layout, input method integration, screen-reader accessibility hooks, right-to-left support). While miscellaneous Rust libraries exist to address some of these issues (e.g., Parley for text layout), developers still have to wire them into a consistent user experience.

The cost of a will varies dramatically based on how you create it and how complex your estate is. Here is a comprehensive comparison of every method, from free options to premium attorney packages.

Several factors push will costs toward the higher end of each range:.

The will vs trust decision is primarily a financial calculation: does the upfront cost of a trust save more than it costs by avoiding probate?

According to recent reports, when you die with only a will (no trust), your estate must go through probate — a court-supervised process where a judge validates your will, your executor inventories assets, debts are paid, and remaining assets are distributed. Probate costs include:.

Probate also takes 6-18 months on average and is a public proceeding — anyone can look up your will, your assets, and who inherited what.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$5,000 upfront but avoids probate entirely. The math is straightforward:.

Sources indicate that for most FI-focused households who are building wealth toward financial independence, the trust pays for itself many times over. If your net worth exceeds $100,000-$200,000 and you own real estate, a trust is almost certainly the better financial decision.

It has been revealed that even with a trust, you still need a pour-over will — a short document that catches any assets not transferred into the trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. You also still need a healthcare directive and durable power of attorney. Most estate initiative packages include all four documents together.

The sticker price of a will is only part of the total cost of estate planning. Several hidden costs catch people off guard:.

The FI-optimized approach to estate planning minimizes cost without sacrificing protection:.

According to recent reports, start with an online will now. A $159 Trust & Will plan gives you a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney today. Do not let perfect be the enemy of done — having a basic will is infinitely better than having no will while you save up for an attorney.

It has been revealed that upgrade to a trust when your net worth exceeds $200,000. At this point, the probate avoidance savings justify the $1,500-$3,500 cost of adding a trust.

Shop attorney fees aggressively. Estate planning is a competitive market. Get quotes from at least three attorneys. Many offer flat-fee packages, and prices can vary by 50-100% for the same work in the same city. Ask specifically whether the quote includes trust funding assistance and deed transfers.

Sources indicate that use online services for updates. Rather than paying an attorney $200-$500 for a codicil, many online platforms let you update your will for free or for a small annual subscription ($19-$39/year). Trust & Will, for example, includes one year of free updates.

Bundle documents. An estate strategy package (will + trust + POA + healthcare directive) typically costs 20-40% less than purchasing each document separately. If you are going to see an attorney, get everything done in one engagement.

Here is the counterintuitive truth: the most expensive estate proposal is the one you never create. Dying without a will (intestate) triggers state default rules that may not match your wishes, longer and more expensive probate proceedings, and potential family conflict. For parents of minor children, it means a judge — not you — decides who raises your kids. The $0-$259 cost of an online will is trivially small compared to these consequences.

While these free options work for simple estates, you may want to pay $99-$259 for a more comprehensive online service that includes healthcare directives and power of attorney.

Attorneys charge $300-$750 for a simple will and $750-$1,500 for a complex will with special provisions. A complete estate blueprint package (will, trust, power of attorney, healthcare directive) runs $1,500-$5,000. Fees vary significantly by location — attorneys in major metros charge 2-3 times more than attorneys in smaller cities for the same work. Always ask for a flat fee rather than hourly billing for estate planning.

Major online will makers like Trust & Will, Nolo WillMaker, and LegalZoom produce documents that are legally valid in all 50 states and cover the same core elements an attorney would include. The difference is that an attorney can provide customized advice, handle complex situations, and anticipate issues specific to your state law. If your estate is simple, an online will is functionally equivalent. If your situation has any complexity, the attorney consultation is worth the additional cost.

According to recent reports, online services typically include free updates for one year and then charge $19-$39 per year for ongoing access. An attorney charges $100-$500 for a codicil (formal amendment) or $300-$1,000 to draft a new will. For minor changes, a codicil is sufficient. For major changes (new spouse, additional children, significant asset changes), creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of conflicting instructions.

It has been revealed that if your estate is under $100,000-$200,000 with no real estate, a will alone is often sufficient. Once your net worth exceeds $200,000 or you own real property, a revocable living trust typically saves more in probate avoidance ($15,000-$70,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) than it costs ($1,500-$5,000). A trust also provides privacy, avoids the 6-18 month probate timeline, and manages your assets if you become incapacitated. For most FI-focused households building significant wealth, a trust is the better long-term choice.

It has been revealed that the most expensive part of estate planning is NOT the documents — it is probate. Probate costs 3-7% of your estate value ($15,000-$70,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) and takes 6-18 months. By comparison, even the most expensive estate plan package ($5,000-$10,000) is a fraction of what your family would spend navigating probate without a trust. The second most expensive mistake is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, which can send six or seven figures to the wrong person with no legal recourse.

The cost of a will ranges from $0 to $10,000+ depending on your method and complexity, but the most expensive option is always having no will at all. For most FI-focused households, start with an online will for $0-$259 to get basic protection in place immediately. As your net worth grows beyond $200,000, invest $1,500-$5,000 in a comprehensive estate proposal with a revocable living trust — the probate savings alone deliver a 300-1,000% return. Update your beneficiary designations today (free), review your plan every 3-5 years, and remember: the goal of estate planning is not to create perfect documents. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, drew DeVault has unveiled that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated.
  • I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
  • Sources indicate that we recommend that Redict owners switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.

In a recent development, drew DeVault has unveiled that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

Sources indicate that we recommend that Redict owners switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Industry observers note that structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

It has been revealed that note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:.

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

According to recent reports, the full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

Sources indicate that we use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:.

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:.

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:.

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:.

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

It has been revealed that after GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it indicates that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

Verifying formal models of Raft implementations

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antithesis

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.
  • Industry observers note that at Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems.
  • In this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.

Industry observers note that at Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems. But Antithesis can also help eliminate certain classes of bugs by using a combination of AI and formal methods to prove the correctness of complex design choices.

In this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp. Although theyâre implementing the same protocol, there are significant differences in the approaches the two use. We used AI, TLA+, and Antithesis to formally model the two libraries with trace validation. We iterated between model checking, Antithesis testing, and proof attempts, each of which exposed bugs in the code or gaps in the model. We patched bugs and refined the model until it was provable, and until every test run was conformant.

Our model handles several extensions to the core Raft algorithm including pre-votes, snapshots, leadership transfers, and, for etcd-raft only: read indexes for linearizability, async storage writes, and membership changes (where etcdâs implementation intentionally deviates from the Raft paper).

Recent findings suggest that the final proofs establish core Raft safety properties such as Election Safety, Leader Completeness, and State-Machine Safety. In other words, our process established that once we applied the workarounds and fixes needed, the specific designs (scoped to the features we modeled) embodied in HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft actually offer the same guarantees that the Raft paper does. We make the artifacts available for open review:.

Earlier this year, we wrote about how we keep finding bugs in every major Raft implementation we test with Antithesis. This was surprising, because the underlying Raft protocol has been extensively studied, formally specified, and rigorously proven correct (under a set of assumptions). In that post, we pointed out that many implementations subtly deviate from those assumptions, re-design the algorithm for performance, and/or extend the core Raft protocol with unverified extensions â thereby introducing bugs.

Since then, advances in AI have made automated theorem proving and formal verification of complex systems much more scalable, making it feasible to connect a specification to its implementation. So we set out to formally verify not just the core Raft protocol, but the specific designs implemented by production Raft libraries, incorporating custom data structures, different modes of concurrency, and various extensions such as pre-votes, leadership transfers, snapshots, and (in the case of etcd-raft) membership changes.

Recent findings suggest that A key challenge in applying formal methods is to identify a level of abstraction that both allows us to reason mathematically about desired properties, and bridges the gap between specification and implementation. We are not yet at the point of reasoning directly at the level of assembly instructions or even programming language semantics in order to verify distributed safety properties in production systems.

Both Anthropic/Theoremâs OSS-Verify and Google DeepMindâs AlphaProof Code only model single-threaded assembly code; whereas distributed systems are concurrent.

The most widely used approach models the software as a state-transition system in a specification language such as TLA+, and checks invariants over these transitions for finite state spaces. TLA+ models can either be hand-written by experts, or these days, inferred directly from the code using AI. This approach has its own limitations, but is increasingly popular. The next challenge, then, is showing that the TLA+ model corresponds to the actual software that will run in production.

For our demonstration, we used Claude Fable 5.2 to automatically infer TLA+ models from the implementations of HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft and then manually reviewed the safety properties declared in the specifications.

The etcd-raft repository has a TLA+ model crafted for trace validation that is now out of date, and is not designed for ease of proof. The Specular project produced models of etcd-raft and hashicorp-raft, but those models are designed for trace validation, not ease of proof, and the TLAPS leaderboard indicates that they remain unsolved as of 20 Nov 2026.

Industry observers note that we had to manually provide guidance on which features to model or leave out, what scenarios to specify for model checking, and make one refinement to the auto-generated safety properties. While AI is generally bad at inferring properties, in this case we simply instructed the agent to express the core safety properties defined in the Raft paper.

Thatâs where Antithesis helps.

It has been revealed that we used the recently introduced Antithesis plugin to automatically set up a test cluster, an input-generating workload designed to handle all the features captured in the model, and assertions that correspond to the modelâs safety properties. The software was then tested under fault injection while being fed random inputs, exercising various code paths and thread / message interleavings.

It has been revealed that for this demonstration, we developed a lightweight trace validation kit that allowed the software running in Antithesis to emit structured log events that correspond to state transitions in the TLA+ specification. Any test execution that produced a trace that did not conform to some path in the model got flagged. A non-conformant trace could indicate incorrect instrumentation of the trace logging itself, or more seriously, a modeling error or a real bug in the system. We instructed our AI agent to diagnose which one of these it might be, using Antithesis as necessary, and continue iterating until the traces and the inferred model converged.

For both Raft models, the specification expresses the following safety properties, taken directly from the Raft paper:.

Before trying to prove anything, we verified that these invariants hold on bounded instances using TLC, the standard TLA+ model checker. These instances, also synthesized by our AI agent, specify various bounds: clusters are usually three nodes, a single client value, at most a couple of terms of leader election, logs that are limited to a few entries, with only a handful of network messages in flight. These bounds sound tiny, but theyâre sufficient to create several interesting cases: competing elections, a deposed leader still replicating, log entries overwritten and re-replicated, crashes in the middle of an operation, etc. We also model checked various configurations of the Raft libraries, e.g. with pre-vote or snapshotting features enabled and disabled. These âsmallâ instances can reach a state space of over 1.6 million states, which TLC explores exhaustively. We also included some larger problems which were only checked via random simulation. If model checking triggered a safety violation, we attempted to reproduce it as an assertion failure locally or in Antithesis; if the software couldnât exhibit the behavior, the model had to be tightened.

Overall, our process was an iterative loop consisting of model checking (flagging invariant violations), trace validation (flagging deviations), model refinement (to fix design flaws or conformance), and software patching (to fix bugs).

In a recent development, in some ways, this approach is similar to and inspired by Specular. However, given their goal of finding bugs, Specularâs approach involved using AI to identify buggy scenarios before writing models, which meant that static analysis was doing a lot of the heavy lifting. In contrast, our models are intended to be more general and prove safety of the full design.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, we encountered bugs in both systems, including previously known open issues such as hashicorp/raft#695 and etcd-io/raft#551, as well as new ones such as hashicorp/raft#746 and etcd-io/raft#558. In our internal repository, we applied a total of 7 patches across the two implementations. In each case, our goal was to make the system and model pass both verification and validation.

We also encountered a few additional crash bugs, but those donât violate safety.

But bounded model checking only indicates the absence of bugs in a small state space. The only way to get assurance for unbounded input sizes is via rigorous mathematical proof.

Industry observers note that there are two good techniques for proving invariants correct for the whole specification: using a theorem prover integrated into TLA+ called TLAPS, or by translating the model into Veil, a library for the Lean proof assistant for modeling state-transition systems. We used both, delegating the task of proof construction to Claude Fable 5.2.

We used Veilâs official tla-to-veil LLM skill for the model translation, and the recommended approach of validating this via bounded equivalence checking, using TLC and Veilâs own model checker, on our previously stored instances.

Industry observers note that ideally, a TLAPS proof provides the best assurance, since it can attest to safety properties defined on the TLA+ model itself. However, we decided to translate TLA+ to Veil and attempt proofs in Lean. Why? As described in the previous section, our process was extremely iterative, involving several steps of model refinement. We wanted to use the proof engine as additional feedback in that process, feeding it any candidate specifications on which bounded model checking and trace validation both succeeded. We found Leanâs interactive tactic paradigm, predictable performance, and persistent kernel-checked proof terms to be key benefits in this iterative process.

In a recent development, on one occasion, a model of etcd-raftâs membership change as implemented could not be proven correct, revealing a complex bug whose trigger was beyond the state space that bounded model checking explores. In such situations, we could use the Antithesis plugin to attempt to synthesize a workload to reproduce the counter-example.

Antithesis also helped in the proof construction process. When working on challenging parts of the proof, Claude hypothesized several intermediate invariants which if true would lead to a straightforward proof strategy. The agent then used Antithesis to rapidly check if those invariants held true in test runs, and discarded them if run-time assertions failed. Antithesis thus made the proof construction phase more efficient.

Sources indicate that once we converged on a state where the safety properties were fully provable in Lean and the model was passing trace validation with Antithesis, we froze the specification and asked agents to prove the same invariants on the TLA+ spec directly with TLAPS. This last step wasnât strictly necessary, but eliminated any shadow of doubt concerning the Lean proofs and the TLA+ spec.

End-to-end, the work on each library cost less than $1,200 in Claude Fable tokens and approximately 2000 Antithesis compute-hours.

Less, we should note, than the prepaid allowance in a single month of Antithesis Teams.

It has been revealed that note that our final proofs verify formal models of the implementation, not the code itself. However, we can gain confidence about the modelâs fidelity based on the trace validation performed with the extensive test coverage that Antithesis provides, including fault injection such as network partitions and node crashes. To strengthen assurance even further, our iterative process involved several steps of mutation testing, including: mutating the specification to check that the proofs fall through, mutating stored test logs to ensure that trace validation fails, and mutating the software itself to ensure that everything breaks.

The models still make several assumptions about the environment, which limits the reach of verification. For example, both Raft libraries provide pluggable interfaces for local persistent storage. In our test workloads, we use BoltDB for storage and the models assume that no single write (e.g., a log entry or tuple of raft state) is ever torn or corrupted, which BoltDB guarantees. A crash can still fall between two writes.

Our work also leaves out several library features which we have not modeled, such as lease-based reads for etcd-raft (because it depends on wall-clock timing), async heartbeats for hashicorp-raft (because it is known to be very very buggy; really), and membership changes for hashicorp-raft (because we were exhausted from patching bugs in the simpler core). Finally, we only verify safety properties and ignore liveness in this prototype. A comprehensive list of assumptions and limitations is provided in the associated artifactâs README.

Recent findings suggest that given our reputation as âa fuzzing companyâ, formal methods might seem like an odd direction for us to explore. But we see ourselves less as âa fuzzing companyâ and more as a correctness manufacturer. We need a wide range of different approaches if we want to build truly robust systems. Each technique compensates for the weaknesses of the others. Moreover, they amplify each otherâs strengths. The first property-based testing framework, QuickCheck, derived test inputs from a functionâs static type. Many of our customers use both testing and formal methods, so we want to make the two techniques work better together.

Industry observers note that the biggest weakness of formal specification is that it proves the design correct, but doesnât guarantee that the code we implemented actually matches the design. Trace validation uses the strengths of tests to compensate for the core weakness of formal specification. Validation works best if our tests can reach wildly unusual system states, which aligns well with our core technology.

According to recent reports, how formal specification can help testing is relatively less explored, but there are some opportunities here too. We often find that newcomers to property-based testing struggle to describe the properties for their system. But they can describe a high-level outline of what the system essentially does. With trace validation, we can potentially turn that outline into a property to test!

Recent findings suggest that all that said, this is an early research project. We could easily map trace logs to spec behaviors because the code and spec were at roughly the same level of abstraction, with a close correlation between lines of Go and lines of TLA+. Most real-world specs, though, are two levels of abstraction above the code they model. This is because 1) TLA+ can do things impossible in a real system, like make truly arbitrary nondeterministic choices, and 2) the spec can simplify implementation details that donât affect the essential design. These features make specification more powerful, but also make trace validation harder.

Think of this as us demonstrating a medicine works on mice, but we havenât yet done a human trial. More work is needed, work which weâre now doing at Antithesis. Stay tuned to see where it ends up.

In formal specification (like with TLA+), we write highly abstract blueprints, or specifications, of systems and find bugs in those blueprints directly. Once weâve found and fixed all the bugs, we can be confident our real system isnât going to have certain design complications.

Recent findings suggest that but how do we know that the code we write actually corresponds to the design we verified? This is one of the major unsolved problems of formal specification, and the solution we used here trace validation (also called âtrace checkingâ). This was first publicly described in the MongoDB paper eXtreme Modeling in Practice. The authors took logged events in the production system, converted them into a sequence of states, and checked if that sequence was possible in the blueprint. If not possible, then the implementation must be doing something forbidden by the blueprint, so there is a divergence between the implementation and spec.

Recent findings suggest that itâs easier to see this with a concrete example. Say we have this pseudocode as our specification:.

By either-or, I mean that exactly one of the two will happen each iteration, but the decision logic is an implementation detail I donât care about. This spec also has the property that, after every loop iteration, passed + failed == i.

Now hereâs one conforming implementation:.

According to recent reports, while the practical way this works is very different than just arbitrary incrementing variables, itâs still the same thing in essence, and we should expect that every sensor either gets added to the set or marked as broken. To do trace validation, we first add some logs to the code:.

It has been revealed that we run this program and it prints âloop passed loop failedâ. We can convert that to a behavior of the spec. If we denote a state as (i, passed, failed), the corresponding sequence of states would be [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1)]. That is valid under the behavior, so this trace conforms to the spec.

Now if we make a diverging change like this:.

In a recent development, itâs now possible to run this and see the logs âloop loopâ. The corresponding behavior, [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0)] is impossible in the spec, so this would fail trace checking and reveal a divergence between the code and spec.

Sources indicate that thatâs how it all works in principle, anyway. Thereâs a lot of technical challenges with getting this working practically. For example, how are we supposed to know that a network timeout may give us an invalid trace, and how are we actually supposed to trigger it? And the answer to that is a combination of the techniques that we use in Antithesis: deterministic simulation testing and fuzzing. But those are things that we talk about in detail in other articles.

Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.
  • On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.
  • Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No financial details, but plenty of other clues.

Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.

On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.

Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.

Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers.

Recent findings suggest that “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.”.

Mastercard previously noted that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program.

Sources indicate that according to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said.

It has been revealed that it’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker.

Industry observers note that plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text,  and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26.

Industry observers note that “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he remarked. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.”.

The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published.

All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security tech giant Sentra.

In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

Sources indicate that N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker remarked, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.”.

Sources indicate that qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®.

Breaking: NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • It has been revealed that neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

It has been revealed that neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Industry observers note that many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

Recent findings suggest that we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

According to recent reports, pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

In a recent development, to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

Recent findings suggest that we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

In a recent development, viDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

Sources indicate that † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

Sources indicate that we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Customers can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Recent findings suggest that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding fresh documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

Recent findings suggest that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Industry observers note that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

In a recent development, neoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

Industry observers note that neoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Firm for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Tech Report: PostgreSQL 19 Released

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Postgresql

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today confirmed the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.
  • It has been revealed that mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale.
  • "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today confirmed the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.

It has been revealed that mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale. This release introduces the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command so people can optimize tables for their current workload without disruption to ongoing operations. PostgreSQL 19 gives users better control over plan stability and query performance with the newly introduced pg_plan_advice extension. Developers will find many delightful features in this release, from support for "read-your-writes" consistency on standbys to "get or create" behavior that saves a network round trip.

"For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team. "PostgreSQL 19 continues that commitment to reliability, giving customers new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and to build applications that span multiple systems.".

PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from 30 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes.

Tables that receive many updates and deletes can build up unused space, known as "bloat," which can also significantly impact query performance. The VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands were previously used to handle this, but had tradeoffs, including preventing access to the table until the cleanup finished. PostgreSQL 19 introduces the REPACK command, which reclaims this space and can reorder a table's data to match an index, and with REPACK (CONCURRENTLY), can do so without blocking reads or writes. REPACK replaces the VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands, both of which remain available for compatibility.

Recent findings suggest that the PostgreSQL query planner usually picks an efficient strategy for each query, but the plan can change as your data changes, and sometimes the newly introduced plan is slower. PostgreSQL 19 adds the pg_plan_advice extension, which allows stabilization of plan choices and the ability to experiment with different plans using the "plan advice" mini-language. The companion pg_stash_advice extension stores advice and automatically applies it to queries based on their query identifier, so you can fix a slow plan without changing your application.

Sources indicate that postgreSQL 19 also helps autovacuum keep up on busy systems. Autovacuum can now vacuum indexes using parallel workers, controlled by the new autovacuum_max_parallel_workers setting, and uses a new scoring system to decide which tables to process first. Queries that read a table can now automatically mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map during execution, reducing the work that future vacuums need to do. Additionally, vacuumdb --analyze-only now analyzes partitioned tables when no tables are specified.

This release adds fresh views for monitoring workloads, including pg_stat_lock for per-lock-type statistics, pg_stat_recovery for recovery status, and pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to show how autovacuum prioritizes tables. The new IO option for EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the matching auto_explain setting report asynchronous I/O activity. PostgreSQL 19 also reports the amount of WAL written for full-page images in pg_stat_wal, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL), and in vacuum and analyze log events.

Previously, PostgreSQL often required people to restart their server to enable logical replication, which could be disruptive in production workloads. PostgreSQL 19 simplifies logical replication initialization by automatically raising the effective WAL level to logical when you create the first logical replication slot. You can see the WAL level in use with the new effective_wal_level setting.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL 19 also adds logical replication of sequence values, which you can publish using FOR ALL SEQUENCES with CREATE PUBLICATION. CREATE PUBLICATION also adds an EXCEPT clause to exclude tables when publishing FOR ALL TABLES, and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION can now get its connection settings from a foreign server, such as one defined with postgres_fdw, using the SERVER clause. Additionally, the newly introduced retain_dead_tuples subscription option lets PostgreSQL detect updates that conflict with a concurrent delete, and these conflicts are counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats.

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the upcoming WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL 19 also improves queries on foreign tables. With the newly introduced import_stats option, postgres_fdw can import table statistics from the remote server when you run ANALYZE, instead of sampling rows from the remote table, which helps the query planner choose better plans.

PostgreSQL 19 adds INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, which lets the RETURNING clause return existing rows that conflict with an insert, simplifying the common "get or create" pattern. COPY can now output data as JSON, including as a single JSON array, and the SQL/JSON path language adds string methods such as lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part(), and btrim(). Additionally, the lead(), lag(), first_value(), last_value(), and nth_value() window functions can now skip NULL values using IGNORE NULLS. The random() function can now also generate random dates and timestamps within a range.

This release also makes many workloads faster without changes to your application. PostgreSQL 19 improves the performance of foreign key checks, which in testing made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster, and adds more query planner optimizations, such as converting NOT IN clauses to more efficient anti-joins when NULL values are not present, and performing eager aggregation before joins to reduce the number of rows to process. PostgreSQL 19 also builds on the asynchronous I/O subsystem added in PostgreSQL 18. When io_method is set to worker (the default), PostgreSQL now automatically adjusts the number of I/O workers between the newly introduced io_min_workers and io_max_workers settings, which replace the io_workers setting. There are also scalability improvements when using LISTEN and NOTIFY to exchange notifications in multi-channel workloads.

Finally, the upcoming password_expiration_warning_threshold setting warns users when their password is about to expire.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL 19 adds server-side support for Server Name Indication (SNI), letting a single PostgreSQL server present a different TLS certificate based on the hostname a client connects to. You can map hostnames to their certificates and keys in the new pg_hosts.conf file. PostgreSQL 19 also now issues a warning after a successful md5 password authentication, which you can turn off with the md5_password_warnings setting. md5 password authentication was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and will be removed in a future release. If you require password-based authentication, use SCRAM authentication. This release also removes support for RADIUS authentication.

Just-in-time compilation (JIT) is now disabled by default, as the cost estimates PostgreSQL used to decide when to use it proved unreliable. If you run many large analytical queries, you may want to enable JIT. When PostgreSQL is built with LZ4 support, the default TOAST compression method is now lz4.

Industry observers note that many other new features and improvements have been added to PostgreSQL 19 that may also be helpful for your use cases. Please see the release notes for a complete list of new and changed features.

In a recent development, postgreSQL is the world's most advanced open source database, with a global community of thousands of consumers, contributors, companies and organizations. Since its beginnings at the University of California, Berkeley over 40 years ago, PostgreSQL has continued with an unmatched pace of development. PostgreSQL's mature feature set not only matches top proprietary database systems, but exceeds them in advanced database features, extensibility, security, and stability.

For explanations of the above features and others, please see the following resources:.

There are several ways you can download PostgreSQL 19, including:.

Other tools and extensions are available on the PostgreSQL Extension Network.

PostgreSQL 19 comes with HTML documentation as well as man pages, and you can also browse the documentation online in both HTML and PDF formats.

According to recent reports, postgreSQL uses the PostgreSQL License, a BSD-like "permissive" license. This OSI-certified license is widely appreciated as flexible and business-friendly, since it does not restrict the use of PostgreSQL with commercial and proprietary applications. Together with multi-firm support and public ownership of the code, our license makes PostgreSQL very popular with vendors wanting to embed a database in their own products without fear of fees, vendor lock-in, or changes in licensing terms.

Postgres, PostgreSQL, and the Elephant Logo (Slonik) are all registered trademarks of the PostgreSQL Community Association. If you wish to use these marks, you must comply with the trademark policy.

Sources indicate that postgreSQL enjoys the support of numerous companies, who sponsor developers, provide hosting resources, and give us financial support. See our sponsors page for some of these project supporters.

There is also a large community of companies offering PostgreSQL Support, from individual consultants to multinational companies.

If you wish to make a financial contribution to the PostgreSQL Global Development Group or one of the recognized community non-profit organizations, please visit our donations page.
